name: Aruba
summary: Aruba licenses captive insurers through the Centrale Bank van Aruba under the State Decree on Captive Insurance Companies, AB 2002 no. 50, made under the State Ordinance on the Supervision of the Insurance Business. The central legislation register text dated 30 September 2015, included in the Bank's captive manual, records amendment AB 2015 no. 47. The decree defines a captive as an insurer that insures or reinsures risks which exclusively or predominantly arise from the business or profession of shareholders or members of enterprises associated in a group, or of participants in a joint venture. It distinguishes pure, association, rent-a-captive, and other captives. The solvency margin is at least Afl. 300,000 for a pure captive, Afl. 500,000 for an association captive, and Afl. 1,000,000 for a rent-a-captive. For any other captive the Bank sets a margin between Afl. 300,000 and Afl. 1,000,000. The application fee is Afl. 1,000. Article 12 of the 30 September 2015 text caps the annual supervisory charge at Afl. 7,500 for each captive. The English translation and the admission policy in the same manual still say Afl. 3,000, which is the cap before AB 2015 no. 47. The Bank's 2024 Annual Statistical Digest, issued on 2 July 2025, counts 3 captive insurance companies at the end of 2024. The Bank's public register lists Bancarib Real Insurance Aruba N.V., MCB Risk Insurance N.V., and Mondis Manufacturers Insurance Company N.V. Day-to-day management must be determined by at least one natural person who resides in Aruba, and the financial administration is kept at an office in Aruba. The decree does not impose a premium tax. A captive may not cover motor-vehicle legal liability. The Bank does not publish a staff count or a licensing-day standard. Supervision enquiries go to supmanager@cbaruba.org.
legislation: State Decree on Captive Insurance Companies (Landsbesluit bijzondere bedrijfsrisicoverzekeraars), AB 2002 no. 50, as amended by AB 2015 no. 47, under the State Ordinance on the Supervision of the Insurance Business, AB 2000 no. 82
applicable_legislation: The decree was made on 7 May 2002 to implement sections 2, fourth paragraph, 14, fourth paragraph, and 31 of the State Ordinance on the Supervision of the Insurance Business. The Bank's captive manual reproduces the central legislation register text dated 30 September 2015, which lists amendment AB 2015 no. 47, together with an unofficial English translation of the 2002 text. Definitions and the four groups are sections 1 and 2. Licensing conditions, the resident manager, and the Aruba office are section 5. Annual accounts and the actuarial report are section 6. The solvency margin is section 8. The application fee is section 11 and the annual charge is section 12. The admission policy and the directives in the manual are the Bank's published supervisory policy. The State Ordinance text in the manual is the register text of 11 January 2017 and lists amendments through AB 2016 no. 53. No later amendment of AB 2002 no. 50 was identified in the Bank's captive manual.

min_capital.Pure captive: A solvency margin of at least Afl. 300,000 (section 8, first paragraph). A pure captive and an association captive insure or reinsure no risks other than those of their shareholders or members, respectively (section 2). The Bank's admission policy describes a pure captive as a wholly owned or controlled company that insures or reinsures only the risks of its non-insurance parent or affiliated companies.
min_capital.Association captive: A solvency margin of at least Afl. 500,000 (section 8). The admission policy applies that figure to an association or industrial captive and describes an association or industry captive as owned by a group of industrial or commercial companies, or by members of a professional association, and established to insure or reinsure the risks of its shareholders. The decree's category is the association captive. It does not use a separate industrial-captive label.
min_capital.Rent-a-captive: A solvency margin of at least Afl. 1,000,000 (section 8). A rent-a-captive insures or reinsures no risks other than those of the participating institutions (section 2). The admission policy describes it as a company that provides captive facilities to others for a fee while protecting itself from losses under their programs.
min_capital.Other captive: A minimum solvency margin fixed by the Bank, between Afl. 300,000 and Afl. 1,000,000 (section 8). The admission policy gives examples rather than separate statutory floors: a special purpose vehicle formed to reinsure a specific risk with risk capital from the capital markets; an agency captive owned by brokers or agents that reinsures a portion of the insurance they sell; and a quasi profit center or open-market captive that primarily insures or reinsures its parent or affiliates and may also insure unrelated parties or assume open-market reinsurance up to 25 percent of the risk portfolio.
min_capital.Additional margin and form: The Bank may prescribe an additional solvency margin based on the type, magnitude, and nature of the risks (section 8, second paragraph). The margin may be maintained in cash or in an irrevocable guarantee issued by a bank established in Aruba that holds a licence under section 4 or 24 of the State Ordinance on the Supervision of the Credit System, AB 1998 no. 16. The Bank's solvency directive states that the minimum margin should at all times be held or invested in Aruba and lists the admissible assets that may cover it, including Aruba government treasury bonds and specified Aruba debt, subject to the Bank's prior approval of valuation and distribution, a pledge to the Bank, and custody at a credit institution the Bank supervises. The admission policy states that the exchange rate of the Aruban florin is fixed at US$1.00 = Afl. 1.79.

tax_notes: The State Decree on Captive Insurance Companies does not impose a premium tax or an insurance-premium tax return. The charges in sections 11 and 12 are an application fee and an annual contribution to the Bank's supervisory costs. The Bank's supervisory-role page presents Afl. 30,000 as the supervisory costs passed on yearly to the captive insurance company sector under AB 2002 no. 50, and states that only a small part of actual supervisory cost is charged to the supervised sectors. That table gives a sector amount. It does not state a per-company premium-tax rate. No corporate income-tax rate for a captive is stated in the decree, the admission policy, or the Bank's captive supervision page.
contact_name: Supervision Department, Centrale Bank van Aruba
types_allowed: Other captive insurance companies, with the solvency margin set by the Bank
Captives formed as a limited liability company, a mutual company, an Aruba exempt corporation, or a branch, as listed on the Bank's application form

fees.licensing_incorporation: Section 11 charges Afl. 1,000 for processing an application for a captive licence. The admission policy states the same application fee. Chamber of Commerce registration fees are not set in the decree.
fees.annual_fees: Section 12 of the central legislation register text dated 30 September 2015 charges each captive, every year, for the Bank's work under the decree. The charge does not exceed Afl. 7,500 and is paid within a period the Bank sets. The first payment is due after the end of the first full financial year following the licence. The unofficial English translation in the Bank's manual, and the admission policy in that manual, still say the annual contribution is a maximum of Afl. 3,000. Those passages reflect the decree before amendment AB 2015 no. 47. The Bank's supervisory-role page states that supervisory costs passed on yearly to the captive insurance company sector are Afl. 30,000. That figure is a sector total in a table of sectors, not a per-company premium tax.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the State Decree on Captive Insurance Companies. The published captive charges are the Afl. 1,000 application fee and the annual supervisory charge capped at Afl. 7,500 in the 30 September 2015 text. No corporate income-tax rate for a captive was stated in the Bank materials reviewed.

annual_filing_requirements: Each year, within six months after the end of the financial year, a captive submits its financial statements to the Bank. The statements of a captive domiciled outside Aruba cover the entire enterprise, wherever it is conducted. The statements are accompanied by a declaration that the information presents a true and fair view, signed by an auditor. Within the same six months the captive submits an actuarial report accompanied by an actuary's certificate (section 6). The Bank may set the model, contents, and bases of both documents. The captive maintains adequate technical provisions, fully covered by assets (section 7). It keeps the financial administration of the insurance business at its office in Aruba and preserves the business documents there for at least ten years (section 5). Day-to-day management is determined by at least one natural person who resides in Aruba. If a representative determines that management, the fit-and-proper provisions of the State Ordinance apply to the representative. The admission policy adds that the captive has a supervisory board, or a comparable body, of at least three natural persons; that at least one managing director of proven ability and experience in insurance, and of good standing, resides in Aruba and is responsible for day-to-day management; and that all board and senior-management appointments require the Bank's prior approval. The same policy says the Bank may fine a captive Afl. 1,000 for each day it fails to file the audited financial statements or the certified actuarial report. A captive may conduct only insurance or reinsurance business, and only life or general business unless the Bank grants an exemption on proof that the two are managed separately. It may not cover the legal liability described in the State Ordinance on Motor Vehicle Liability, AB 1999 no. GT 12. If the solvency margin falls below the required level, or the Bank sees other signs that endanger solvency, the captive submits a financing plan within a period the Bank sets. The Bank may withdraw the licence if the margin is not restored within the approved period. The decree and the Bank's captive pages do not state an in-Aruba board-meeting requirement or a periodic on-site examination interval. The supervision page says oversight is conducted mainly by off-site surveillance and periodic on-site examinations.

name: Bahrain
summary: Bahrain licenses captive insurers through the Central Bank of Bahrain under Volume 3 of the CBB Rulebook. The Bank's insurance page states that the CBB has been the insurance regulator since 2002. The capital-adequacy module is a directive issued under Article 38 of the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law 2006. A captive is Category C1 or Category C2. Category C1 may insure only non-liability risks of its shareholders or of subsidiary or associated companies of those shareholders. Category C2 is limited to the same related risks and may include liability risks if the CBB is satisfied that the activity, capital structure and management protect potential third-party claimants. Captives are not subject to the BD 5 million Tier 1 floor for a Bahraini insurance firm, or the BD 10 million floor where that firm's business is limited to reinsurance. They must keep capital available above the greater of the required solvency margin and a minimum fund of BD 75,000 for Category C1 or BD 300,000 for Category C2. A captive may be a Bahraini special purpose vehicle or one of the other insurance-firm legal forms. The annual licensing fee is a fixed BD 1,000. Central Bank of Bahrain correspondence, November 2026, states that the captive licence application fee is BD 100, non-refundable, and payable on submission through the CBB online application portal (https://www.cbb.gov.bh/application-for-a-license/). After receipt of the required forms and supporting documents, the Bank assesses the application and the proposed business model before determining next steps. That correspondence does not state a processing timeline. The fact sheet counts 1 captive among 21 locally incorporated insurance and reinsurance firms. That sheet dates the wider count of insurance companies and organisations at December 2025 and does not date the captive line separately, or publish new licences, surrenders, or a staff count. Central Bank of Bahrain correspondence, November 2026, points to the CBB Licensing Directory for institutions currently licensed and does not state a captive count, the date of that count, or figures for new licences and surrenders. The solvency-margin percentages in CA-2.1.10 to CA-2.1.12 remain unverified. Licensing enquiries go to licensing@cbb.gov.bh.
legislation: Central Bank of Bahrain Rulebook, Volume 3 (Insurance), including Module CA (Capital Adequacy) and Module CI (Captive Insurance), issued under the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law 2006
applicable_legislation: Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law 2006. Module CA is the CBB directive on capital adequacy of insurance licensees issued under Article 38 of that law. The directive was adopted in January 2007 and the module records a later amendment in January 2011. Category C1 and Category C2, and their minimum funds, are CA-2.1.5 and CA-2.1.6, amended January 2007. The Tier 1 exception for captives is CA-1.2.1, amended January 2007 and October 2007. Legal form is AU-2.1.1 to AU-2.1.3, amended July 2007 and, for the special-purpose-vehicle paragraph, January 2008. The annual licensing fee is AU-6.3.3, added July 2007 and amended July 2013. The Insurance Firm Return is BR-1.1, amended January 2007, with the captive risk-gap and reinsurance information in BR-1.1.6. The captive overview in ES-1.17.3 records the exemptions from quarterly and group financial reporting. The Bank's insurance page states that the CBB has regulated insurance since 2002. Central Bank of Bahrain correspondence, November 2026, refers to the Authorisation Module (AU) of CBB Rulebook Volume 3 (Insurance), May 2026 update, for the applicable licensing requirements, and to the CBB Licensing Directory for institutions currently licensed.

min_capital.Category C1: Minimum fund of BD 75,000 (CA-2.1.5(e)). A Category C1 insurer may insure only the insurance risks, other than liability risk, of its shareholders or of subsidiary or associated companies of its shareholders (CA-2.1.6(e)).
min_capital.Category C2: Minimum fund of BD 300,000 (CA-2.1.5(f)). A Category C2 insurer is restricted to the risks of its shareholders or of their subsidiary or associated companies, and its business may include liability risks if the CBB is satisfied that the activity, capital structure and management provide sufficient protection to potential third-party claimants (CA-2.1.6(f)).
min_capital.Tier 1 capital: Captive insurers are not subject to a minimum Tier 1 capital. A Bahraini insurance firm otherwise maintains minimum Tier 1 capital of BD 5 million, or BD 10 million where its business is limited to reinsurance (CA-1.2.1).
min_capital.Capital available and solvency margin: Every insurance firm must at all times maintain capital available in excess of the greater of the required solvency margin and the minimum fund (CA-1.2.1). The required solvency margin for long-term insurance business is determined under CA-2.1.9, and for general insurance business under CA-2.1.12 (CA-2.1.7). Where the long-term aggregate falls below the minimum fund, the minimum fund is substituted. The percentage components of CA-2.1.10, CA-2.1.11 and CA-2.1.12 were not extracted from the rulebook section retrieved, so they are not restated.
min_capital.Legal form and incorporation capital: A captive's legal status must be a Bahraini special purpose vehicle established to carry out the captive's activities, or a Bahraini joint stock company, a Bahraini branch of an overseas insurance or reinsurance firm, or a Bahraini exempt company that was incorporated and licensed to conduct insurance business before 1 January 2005 (AU-2.1.1 and AU-2.1.2). A Bahraini special purpose vehicle is a closed joint stock company. The rulebook states that the minimum capital required by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to incorporate that company is BD 1,000, and that the captive must still satisfy the Module CA capital requirements (AU-2.1.3).

tax_notes: The CBB Rulebook fee for a captive is a fixed annual licensing fee, not a premium tax. The National Bureau for Revenue states that value-added tax has been charged at the standard rate of 10 percent since 1 January 2022. Its financial-services guidance states that life insurance contracts, life reinsurance contracts and transfers of those contracts are exempt, and that other insurance services, such as medical and motor insurance, are taxable at 10 percent, with travel insurance zero-rated in some cases. Decree-Law No. 11 of 2024 imposes a domestic minimum top-up tax of 15 percent, from 1 January 2025, on multinational enterprises whose annual global revenue is at least EUR 750 million. On 30 December 2025 the Bureau described a draft law, to be referred to the legislature, that would charge 10 percent on profits above BD 200,000 of local companies whose revenue exceeds BD 1 million or whose annual net profit exceeds BD 200,000, with the stated aim of applying it in 2027. The Bureau said a group already within the 15 percent top-up tax would not also pay that 10 percent. The draft is not stated as a tax in force. No captive-specific income-tax exemption was stated on the Bureau pages or in the rulebook modules reviewed.
contact_name: Licensing and Regulatory Policy Directorate, Central Bank of Bahrain
types_allowed: Category C1 captive insurers, limited to non-liability risks of shareholders and of their subsidiary or associated companies

Category C2 captive insurers, limited to related-party risks and permitted to include liability risks where the Central Bank of Bahrain is satisfied that activity, capital and management protect third-party claimants
Captives formed as a Bahraini special purpose vehicle
Captives formed as a Bahraini joint stock company, as a branch of an overseas insurer, or as a Bahraini exempt company incorporated and licensed before 1 January 2005

fees.licensing_incorporation: Central Bank of Bahrain correspondence, November 2026, states that the captive licence application fee is BD 100, non-refundable, and payable on submission through the CBB online application portal (https://www.cbb.gov.bh/application-for-a-license/). The annual licensing fee on grant is the fixed captive fee in AU-6.3.3. The rulebook states that Ministry of Commerce and Industry incorporation capital for a Bahraini special purpose vehicle is BD 1,000. That figure is an incorporation-capital floor, not the CBB licensing fee, and the captive must still meet the Module CA minimum fund.
fees.annual_fees: BD 1,000 fixed annual licensing fee for a captive insurance firm (AU-6.3.3, amended July 2013). An insurance firm that is not a captive pays a fixed annual licensing fee of BD 6,000. The Bank's licensing page publishes the same captive fee of BD 1,000.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the captive licensing-fee rule. Value-added tax is 10 percent on taxable insurance other than exempt life insurance and life reinsurance. A 15 percent domestic minimum top-up tax applies from 1 January 2025 to in-scope multinational enterprises with annual global revenue of at least EUR 750 million. A proposed 10 percent tax on specified local-company profits was described by the National Bureau for Revenue on 30 December 2025 as a draft for the legislature, aimed at 2027, and is not stated as a tax in force.

annual_filing_requirements: An insurance firm prepares and submits an Insurance Firm Return for each financial year within 3 months of the financial year end (BR-1.1.1 and BR-1.1.5). The financial year is 12 months ending on 31 December unless the CBB consents in writing to another period or year end. The period cannot be shorter than 6 months or longer than 18 months (BR-1.1.2). Captive insurers submit additional return information on the risk gap, being the degree to which potential liabilities under the policy limits exceed available assets and the resources available to meet that gap, and on reinsurance providers, limits and claims (BR-1.1.6). The return is submitted on the prescribed form, with an actuary's certificate and report where applicable (BR-1.1.5). It is reviewed under the international standard on related services for agreed-upon procedures, and the review certifies that the information agrees with the books and records and with the audited financial statements (BR-1.1.14). The external auditor's report, in the CBB format, is provided within 4 months of the financial year end (BR-1.1.16). ES-1.17.3 records that captives are exempt from quarterly and group financial reporting and that public-disclosure requirements do not apply to them. The sections reviewed do not state an in-Bahrain board-meeting requirement or a periodic on-site examination interval.

licensing_speed: After receipt of the required forms and supporting documents, the Central Bank of Bahrain assesses the application and the proposed business model before determining next steps (Central Bank of Bahrain correspondence, November 2026). That correspondence does not state a processing timeline.

name: Barbados
summary: Barbados licenses insurers under the Insurance Act, Cap. 310. The Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52 commenced on 1 January 2019, created three licence classes, and repealed the Exempt Insurance Act, Cap. 308A. A Class 1 licensee is an insurance company that underwrites related-party business. A Class 2 licensee includes an insurance company that underwrites third-party risks, and Class 3 covers insurance intermediaries, managers, and holding companies. The Financial Services Commission supervises the sector under the Financial Services Commission Act, 2010-21. The Commission's homepage reported 176 Class 1 licensees at 31 December 2025, compared with 175 at 31 December 2024. It reported 121 Class 2 licensees at 31 December 2025, of which 21 had direct exposure to the Barbadian public, and 815 Class 3 licensees. Class 1 is the related-party population. The Commission does not publish a pure-versus-group split, a cell count, or 2025 figures for new and surrendered Class 1 licences.
legislation: Insurance Act, Cap. 310, as amended by the Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52 (commenced 1 January 2019)
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act, Cap. 310; Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52, which commenced on 1 January 2019 and repealed the Exempt Insurance Act, Cap. 308A; Financial Services Commission Act, 2010-21. Minimum capital and solvency for Class 1 and Class 2 insurers are set out in the Commission's capital and solvency appendix.

min_capital.Class 1 or Class 2, risks and premiums o: BDS $250,000 minimum paid-up share capital in cash for long-term insurance, general insurance, or both, or such other amount as the Commission determines. An equivalent sum in another currency is allowed if the Commission approves it. Capital must be fully paid up in cash.
min_capital.Class 1 or Class 2, risks and premiums i: BDS $3,000,000 long-term; BDS $3,000,000 general; BDS $5,000,000 long-term and general; BDS $1,000,000 motor vehicle only; BDS $1,000,000 industrial life.
min_capital.Segregated cell company, Barbados reinsu: A Class 1 or Class 2 segregated cell company licensed to carry on reinsurance of risks located in Barbados, with premiums originating in Barbados, must have aggregate paid-up capital of BDS $3,000,000, and each cell must have minimum paid-up capital of BDS $500,000.
min_capital.Solvency, risks and premiums outside Bar: In the first financial year, assets must exceed liabilities by BDS $250,000. After that year, assets must exceed liabilities by BDS $250,000 if the preceding year's premium income did not exceed BDS $1,500,000; by one-fifth of that premium income if it exceeded BDS $1,500,000 but did not exceed BDS $10,000,000; or by BDS $2,000,000 plus one-tenth of the amount by which premium income exceeded BDS $10,000,000.

name: Bermuda
summary: Bermuda's captive classes are supervised by the Bermuda Monetary Authority under the Insurance Act 1978. Class 1 is a single-parent general captive writing only the risks of its owners and their affiliates. Class 2 covers multi-owner captives and captives writing no more than 20 percent of net premiums from unrelated risks. Class 3 covers captives writing more than 20 percent, and up to 49 percent, of net premiums from unrelated risks, together with certain third-party writers that are not commercial Class 3A, 3B, or 4 insurers. Class A and Class B are the long-term equivalents of Class 1 and Class 2. The Authority's 2025 annual report gives 2025 register counts of 159 Class 1, 244 Class 2, 180 Class 3, 12 Class A, and 13 Class B insurers, 608 in those captive classes. The 2024 column of the same table is 632 and matches the report's market statistics for the year ended 31 December 2024. Single-parent captives are the Class 1 and Class A counts, 171 in the 2025 column, which is the same pairing the report used for its 31 December 2024 company-type table. Class 3, 180, is the third-party captive category. Class 2 and Class B together are 257 and mix multi-owner captives with captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated premiums, so that pair is not stored as a group-captive count. New captive-class registrations in the 2025 column were 2 Class 1, 5 Class 2, 1 Class 3, 1 Class A, and no Class B, 9 in total. The report does not publish surrenders. Its 2023 captive insight report, published in December 2025, said segregated and incorporated segregated accounts were in excess of 2,000 and that 15 percent of captive-market companies operated as segregated accounts or incorporated segregated accounts companies. That report does not give an exact cell count, and the 2025 annual report does not update it. Captive Review reported on 11 November 2026 that the Authority licensed one captive-class insurer in October 2026, Project Pearl ISAC Ltd as a Class A insurer on 21 October, bringing captive-class formations in the first 10 months of 2026 to eight: two Class 1, three Class 2, one Class 3 and two Class A. That year-to-date figure is not a full-year count and does not replace the 2025 annual report statistics above.
legislation: Insurance Act 1978, and the Insurance Returns and Solvency Regulations 1980
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act 1978, including section 17 on statutory financial statements and section 18 on statutory financial returns; Insurance Returns and Solvency Regulations 1980, Schedule I (general-business solvency margin) and Schedule II (long-term minimum margin of solvency); Bermuda Monetary Authority Act 1969, Fourth Schedule, for fees effective 1 January 2026; Corporate Income Tax Act 2023; Bermuda Monetary Authority Guidance Note, General Business Insurers with Segregated Accounts and Separate Accounts (September 2026), issued under section 2B of the Insurance Act 1978, for financial years commencing on or after 1 January 2027. It applies to limited-purpose and commercial insurers in the general-business licence classes that maintain segregated accounts under the Segregated Accounts Companies Act 2000 or separate accounts permitted for insurers incorporated under a private act. It does not apply to long-term insurers. Incorporated segregated account companies and incorporated segregated account insurers remain under the separate guidance note issued in December 2020. Where this note and the Special Purpose Insurer guidance note issued on 1 July 2020 do not align, the Special Purpose Insurer note takes precedence for that class. The Authority will consider transitional applications in the first year after implementation. Bermuda Monetary Authority Notice, Agreed Upon Procedures for Segregated Account and Separate Account General Business Insurers (23 September 2026).

min_capital.Class 1: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, the greater of a premium-based formula and a reserve-based formula, subject to a $120,000 floor.
min_capital.Class 2: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, subject to a $250,000 floor.
min_capital.Class 3: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, subject to a $1,000,000 floor.
min_capital.Class A: Long-term single-parent captives maintain minimum capital and surplus at least equal to an asset-based formula, subject to a $120,000 floor.
min_capital.Class B: Long-term multi-owner captives, and long-term captives writing no more than 20 percent of net premiums from unrelated risks, maintain minimum capital and surplus at least equal to an asset-based formula, subject to a $250,000 floor.
min_capital.General-business segregated accounts and: For financial years commencing on or after 1 January 2027, each segregated account or separate account must meet the relevant solvency requirements on a stand-alone basis and must maintain capital and liquidity adequate to the risks it assumes, independently of the company's consolidated position. A segregated accounts company must not make underwriting, reserving, or distribution decisions by reference to the consolidated capital position of the company as a whole. The account is to be fully collateralised, financed up to the contract's full maximum aggregate exposure and held to the benefit of the insured, or fully funded, financed up to the reserve provision. Where the account writes fully collateralised business, the collateral must be contributed on or before the insurance contract's effective date. This guidance does not apply to long-term business. Incorporated segregated accounts are addressed separately.

tax_notes: The Insurance Act fee schedule does not impose a premium tax. Captive regulatory cost is the Bermuda Monetary Authority licence fee. The Corporate Income Tax Act 2023 charges Bermuda corporate income tax to Bermuda constituent entities of an in-scope multinational group for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. The Government of Bermuda describes that regime as its implementation of the OECD Pillar II 15 percent minimum tax for multinational groups with annual revenue of EUR 750 million or more. Captives that are not constituent entities of an in-scope group are outside that tax.
types_allowed: Class 2 multi-owner general captives and captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated net premiums
Class 3 captives writing more than 20 percent and up to 49 percent unrelated net premiums
Class B multi-owner long-term captives and long-term captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated net premiums
Segregated accounts companies and incorporated segregated accounts companies

fees.licensing_incorporation: 2026 registration fees in the Bermuda Monetary Authority fee schedule, effective 1 January 2026: Class 1 general business $2,250; Class 2 general business $4,375; Class 3 general business $17,800 where expected gross premium does not exceed $5 million, then $19,800, $22,550, $25,920, and $30,000 at the published premium bands; Class A $13,570; Class B $13,570.
fees.annual_fees: 2026 annual fees, also effective 1 January 2026, match those registration amounts for Class 1 ($2,250), Class 2 ($4,375), Class 3 ($17,800 to $30,000 by gross premium written), Class A ($13,570), and Class B ($13,570). For a segregated accounts company the premium measure combines the general account and the segregated accounts. Annual fees cancelled by deregistration, discontinuance, or merger before 31 March are pro-rated; otherwise the full annual fee is due.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the Insurance Act fee schedule. Bermuda corporate income tax applies only to Bermuda constituent entities of an in-scope multinational group, for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. The Government describes the rate as the OECD Pillar II 15 percent minimum for groups with annual revenue of EUR 750 million or more.

annual_filing_requirements: Under section 17 of the Insurance Act 1978, a Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3 insurer that is not also Class C, D, or E, and a Class A or Class B insurer, files statutory financial statements within six months after the financial year-end, or within a longer period of up to nine months that the Authority allows on application. The statutory financial return under section 18 is filed at the same time. A loss-reserve specialist's opinion is required annually for a Class 3 insurer and every third year for a Class 2 insurer. The Act does not state that opinion for a Class 1 insurer. For a general-business insurer with segregated accounts or separate accounts, in a financial year commencing on or after 1 January 2027, the statutory financial statements include a Schedule of Segregated Accounts for the general account and each cell. The Schedule forms part of the annual statutory filing and is outside the scope of the statutory audit. The annual statutory submission includes a Principal Representative attestation, embedded in the Schedule and signed annually, that the Schedule reflects the position of each segregated account and the company's financial standing and that the collateral covers the associated liabilities. Under the Authority's 23 September 2026 agreed-upon procedures notice, the approved auditor performs those procedures and files the report separately from the statutory audit opinion, concurrently with the annual statutory financial return.

name: British Columbia
summary: British Columbia enacted Canada's first dedicated captive insurance statute in 1987 under the Insurance (Captive Company) Act (RSBC 1996, c. 227) and remains one of two Canadian provinces with standalone captive legislation alongside Alberta. Regulated by the BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA), which succeeded the Financial Institutions Commission (FICOM) in 2019, it permits pure, association, and sophisticated insured captives—the latter requiring insureds to have aggregate annual insurance premiums of at least CAD 500,000. Captives can write nearly all classes of insurance or reinsurance (excluding direct surety and non-fleet automobile) and require a minimum of CAD 200,000 in shareholders' equity and CAD 100,000 in reserves. On 5 November 2026, BCFSA Statutory Approvals confirmed 20 active captives: 16 pure captives, 4 association captives, and 0 sophisticated insured captives. During 2026, 1 captive was licensed and 1 captive wound up.

tax_notes: Subject to BC Insurance Premium Tax on BC risks (4.4% property and fleet auto, 4% general/other, 2% life, accident and sickness) and federal (15%) and provincial (12%) corporate income taxes.
contact_name: Tolga Yalkin, CEO & Superintendent of Financial Institutions

fees.licensing_incorporation: CAD 10,000 application fee for initial registration (effective September 1, 2024 under BC Reg. 183/2024; previously CAD 3,000).

Consent fees: CAD 5,000 amalgamation, CAD 500 change in control, CAD 100 articles amendment.
fees.premium_tax_rate: BC Insurance Premium Tax on taxable BC premiums: 4.4% for property and automobile insurance; 4% for general/other insurance; 2% for life, accident and sickness, and loss-of-wages insurance. Corporate income tax rates: 15% federal, 12% provincial.

annual_filing_requirements: Registration expires 90 days after fiscal year-end and must be renewed annually via BCFSA's IRIS portal on or before 90 days after fiscal year-end, including: renewal application and fee, Captive Insurance Financial Schedule, audited financial statements (prepared under IFRS 17) with auditor's report, independent actuarial report (FCIA), parent/association financial statements, copies of insurance policies, reinsurance agreements, and investment policy. Meeting required in domicile.

The bulletin states that these timelines are a general guideline, can vary with volume and complexity, and that review by the decision maker may affect them. Captive insurance company renewal has a separate 90-day target in the same bulletin.

name: British Virgin Islands
summary: The British Virgin Islands Financial Services Commission licenses insurers under the Insurance Act, 2008, the Insurance Regulations, 2009 and the Regulatory Code, 2009. The Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2015 added Category E, a pure captive that may underwrite related-party business only, and Category F, a captive that underwrites related-party business and a maximum of unrelated business in order to qualify as an insurer under the law of a foreign jurisdiction. A Category C, D, E or F insurer must appoint a licensed insurance manager. A segregated portfolio company that wants an insurance licence is licensed as Category C. Minimum contributed capital under section 130 of the Code is $200,000 where the insurer may carry on any class of long-term business, and $100,000 otherwise. The Financial Services (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2023, in force for these items from 1 April 2023, charge US$1,000 to apply for an insurer's licence, US$2,000 to issue a Category C, D, E or F licence, and US$7,500 to issue a Category C segregated-portfolio-company licence. Annual renewal for Category C, D, E or F runs from US$2,000 to US$7,500 by the preceding year's gross written premium, and a Category C segregated portfolio company pays US$7,500. The 2025 fee amendment did not change those insurance items. The Commission's 2024 annual report chart shows 44 captive insurers at the end of 2024, compared with 45 at the end of 2023, within 103 active insurance entities. Captive gross direct written premium was $75,404,920 and captive total assets were $1,510,902,604. The report does not publish formations, surrenders, a pure-versus-group split, or a staff count. The Insurance Act and the fee regulations do not impose a premium tax, and they do not state a corporate income-tax rate.
legislation: Insurance Act, 2008 (Revised 2020 text published by the Commission), Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2015, Insurance Regulations, 2009, and Regulatory Code, 2009
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act, 2008, as amended by the Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2015 (Act No. 16 of 2015), which inserted Category E and Category F. Licence categories are section 7. Contributed capital is section 10, and the dollar floors are Regulatory Code section 130. The solvency margin is section 12 of the Act and section 131 of the Code. An insurance manager for Category C, D, E or F is section 23. Directors are section 25. Segregated portfolio companies are section 36A. Audited financial statements are sections 56 and 57. Fees are the Financial Services (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2023 (S.I. 2023 No. 5), which substituted the schedule from 1 April 2023. The annual due date remains regulation 2A of the Financial Services (Fees) Regulations, as substituted by S.I. 12 of 2017 and left in place by the 2023 substitution of the schedule. The Financial Services (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025 (S.I. 2025 No. 4), in force on 2 January 2025, amended anti-money-laundering reporting-officer fees and did not amend the insurance items. The Insurance Guidelines, 2016 explain Categories E and F and segregated portfolio licensing. The captive annual return is filed under the Financial Services (Prudential and Statistical Returns) Order, 2009, as described in the Commission's captive-return guidance.

min_capital.Contributed capital, general business: Section 130 of the Regulatory Code sets the minimum contributed capital of a BVI insurer at $100,000 where the insurer is not authorised to carry on any class of long-term business. Section 10 of the Insurance Act requires the insurer to maintain at least the greater of that Code minimum and any higher amount the Commission directs.
min_capital.Contributed capital, long-term business: Section 130 of the Code sets the minimum at $200,000 where the insurer is authorised to carry on any class of long-term business. The same section applies to a BVI insurer that writes both long-term business and property and casualty business, because the long-term limb is triggered by authorisation for any class of long-term business.
min_capital.Solvency margin, general insurer: Section 131 of the Code requires a general insurer to maintain a minimum solvency margin of $100,000 if annual net written premium is less than $500,000; 20 percent of net annual written premium if that premium is greater than $500,000 but less than $5,000,000; and $1,000,000 plus 10 percent of the amount by which annual net written premium exceeds $5,000,000 if that premium is greater than $5,000,000. The section does not state the margin at exactly $500,000 or exactly $5,000,000. In the first financial year the premium measure is the amount projected in the business plan.
min_capital.Solvency margin, long-term insurer: Section 131 of the Code requires a long-term insurer to maintain a minimum solvency margin of $250,000. The insurer must in any event maintain a solvency margin adequate to meet its liabilities, taking into account the nature, size, complexity, structure and diversity of the business and its risk profile.
min_capital.Commission direction: The Commission may direct a higher contributed capital or a higher amount of capital resources, with at least 14 days to comply (Insurance Act, section 10). Section 129 of the Code requires capital resources adequate for the business in addition to the specific contributed-capital and solvency floors.

tax_notes: The Insurance Act and the Financial Services (Fees) Regulations impose licence fees. They do not impose a premium tax. No corporate income-tax rate for a captive, and no statement that the Territory imposes no income tax, was found in the Insurance Act, the Regulatory Code, the Insurance Regulations, the fee regulations, the 2024 annual report, or the Insurance Guidelines reviewed.
contact_name: British Virgin Islands Financial Services Commission
types_allowed: Category E insurers, pure captives limited to related-party business
Category F insurers, captives writing related-party business and a maximum of unrelated business in order to qualify as an insurer under foreign law
Category C insurers, BVI business companies writing insurance that is not domestic business, including reinsurance that is not open-market reinsurance where the licence permits
Category C segregated portfolio companies licensed under section 36A of the Insurance Act and Part VII of the BVI Business Companies Act
Category D insurers, BVI business companies writing reinsurance, including open-market reinsurance
Insurers licensed for both life and health business and property and casualty business where the Commission is satisfied as to resources and the business plan

fees.licensing_incorporation: Under the schedule substituted by the Financial Services (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2023, with effect from 1 April 2023, the application fee for a Category A, B, C, D, E or F insurer's licence is US$1,000. The fee for issuing the licence is US$3,500 for Category A or B, US$2,000 for Category C, D, E or F, and US$7,500 for a Category C segregated portfolio company. An application to vary a licence by adding or removing a class of business, or by converting a category, is US$1,000, and approval of a variation is US$1,500 or US$2,000 for a conversion. An insurance manager's application fee is US$500 and the fee for issuing that licence is US$2,000. Registry incorporation fees are not set in the insurance rows of the schedule. The Commission's website FAQ still shows a single captive annual figure and is not the fee instrument used here.
fees.annual_fees: Annual fees under the Insurance Act are due no later than 28 February (regulation 2A of the Financial Services (Fees) Regulations). The 2023 schedule sets annual renewal for a Category C, D, E or F licensee, by total gross written premiums of the preceding year, at US$2,000 where premiums are $500,000 or less, US$3,000 from $500,001 to $999,999, US$3,500 from $1,000,000 to $2,400,000, US$4,500 from $2,400,001 to $4,999,999, US$6,000 from $5,000,000 to $9,999,999, and US$7,500 at $10,000,000 and above. A Category C segregated portfolio company pays US$7,500. An insurance manager's annual renewal is US$2,000. The Financial Services (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025 did not change these insurance amounts.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the Insurance Act or the fee schedule. The regulatory charge is the fixed or premium-banded licence fee. No corporate income-tax rate was stated in the Commission legislation and reports reviewed.

annual_filing_requirements: A BVI insurer submits financial statements within 6 months of the financial year end, or within a shorter prescribed period, together with an auditor's report and any report made to members (Insurance Act, section 57). The statements are approved by the directors and signed by at least one director (section 56). The insurer appoints an auditor approved by the Commission (section 61). The Commission may extend the section 57 period by up to 3 months in aggregate (section 59). A licensee in Category C, D, E or F also files the Captive Insurance Business Annual Return for the previous calendar year on or before 31 March, under the Commission's guidance on the Financial Services (Prudential and Statistical Returns) Order, 2009. The return goes to insurancereturns@bvifsc.vg. An extension of up to 30 days may be requested at least seven days before the deadline. Monetary amounts in the return are reported in US dollars. A Category C, D, E or F insurer appoints and at all times has an insurance manager that holds an insurance manager's licence, with the Commission's prior written approval (section 23). A BVI insurer has at least two directors, each an individual (section 25). A segregated portfolio company is licensed under section 36A. The Act does not state an in-Territory board-meeting requirement in the sections reviewed. The 20 March 2026 public statement directs general contact to commissioner@bvifsc.vg. The Commission's division email list also publishes Insurance@bvifsc.vg for the Insurance Division.

The guidelines do not state that number of days. The Insurance Act does not state a licensing-day standard.

name: Cayman Islands
summary: The Cayman Islands is the world's second-largest captive domicile and the leading domicile for healthcare captives, regulated by the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority (CIMA) under the Insurance Act, 2010, as amended. International insurers are licensed as Class B (B(i) where at least 95 percent of net premiums come from related business, B(ii) where more than 50 percent are related, and B(iii) where 50 percent or less are related), Class C (fully collateralised insurance-linked structures) or Class D (open-market reinsurance). As of Q3 2026, CIMA reported 720 Class B, C and D insurers, writing US$62.3 billion of premium and holding US$202.9 billion of assets. Of that population, 337 were categorised as pure captives and 149 as group captives. Medical malpractice was the primary class of 127 licensees, and North America accounted for 632 licensees (88 percent). Class B segregated portfolio companies numbered 177, with 634 segregated portfolios and 68 portfolio insurance companies; those counts sit inside the 720 and are not additional licensees. In 2025 CIMA issued 42 international licences and cancelled 19. Through the 2026 year to date, issues and cancellations were 28 and 28, leaving the international total at 720. Every captive must appoint a licensed local insurance manager. CIMA states that a complete Class B or Class C application takes six to eight weeks. The Islands levy an annual licence fee rather than a premium tax, and CIMA describes the domicile as having no corporate or personal taxes.
legislation: Insurance Act, 2010 (Law 32 of 2010), as amended, and the Insurance (Capital and Solvency) (Classes B, C and D Insurers) Regulations (2018 Revision)
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act, 2010 (Law 32 of 2010), as amended, including the Insurance (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2024 (Act 14 of 2024); Insurance (Capital and Solvency) (Classes B, C and D Insurers) Regulations (2018 Revision); Insurance (Applications and Fees) Regulations (2026 Revision), as adjusted for Class B(i), (ii) and (iii) by the Insurance (Application and Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025, effective 1 January 2026; Insurance (Portfolio Insurance Companies) Regulations (2026 Revision); Companies Act (2026 Revision) segregated portfolio company provisions.

Class B, C and D insurers also file a capital and solvency return by the prescribed filing date. Annual licence fees are due by 15 January.

name: China
summary: China licenses captive insurers, called captive insurance companies in the National Financial Regulatory Administration's licensing guide, under item 409 of the Decision of the State Council on Setting Administrative Licensing for Administrative Examination and Approval Items That Need to Be Retained, State Council Order No. 412. That decision took effect on 1 July 2004 and assigns approval of the establishment, merger, division, change and dissolution of an exclusive captive organisation. The Administration's 2023 licensing guide, and its 2025 guide, still list the Insurance Law, the Provisions on the Administration of Insurance Companies, the Notice on Matters Concerning the Supervision of Captive Insurance Companies, and the Notice on Further Improving Matters Concerning the Supervision of Captive Insurance Companies as conditions for captive preparation and opening. The full texts of those two notices were not available as live Administration or State Council pages, so their parent-company asset threshold, business-line list and any captive-specific capital formula are not restated. Where the Insurance Law applies, Article 69 requires registered capital of at least RMB 200 million, paid in cash. The supervisor may set a higher floor and may not set a lower one. The Administration's legal-person list as at 31 December 2025 identifies four property insurers whose Chinese or English names identify them as captives: CNPC Captive Insurance, China Railway Captive Insurance, COSCO Shipping Captive Insurance, and Guangdong Energy Captive Insurance. The list does not use a separate captive institution type, and it does not publish formations or surrenders. No captive-specific tax exemption was stated in the Insurance Law text or the licensing guide. Enterprise income tax is 25 percent. Value-added tax on insurance services, as a financial service, is 6 percent for a general taxpayer.
legislation: Decision of the State Council on Setting Administrative Licensing for Administrative Examination and Approval Items That Need to Be Retained, State Council Order No. 412, item 409, and the Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China
applicable_legislation: State Council Order No. 412 was promulgated on 29 June 2004 and took effect on 1 July 2004. Item 409 retains licensing for the establishment, merger, division, change and dissolution of an exclusive captive organisation and a mutual insurance organisation. The decision states that procedures and time limits follow the Administrative License Law. The National Financial Regulatory Administration's licensing guide of 16 June 2023 lists, as conditions for captive preparation and opening, the Insurance Law, the Provisions on the Administration of Insurance Companies, the Notice on Matters Concerning the Supervision of Captive Insurance Companies, the Notice on Further Improving Matters Concerning the Supervision of Captive Insurance Companies, and several general insurer rules on shareholders, plans, articles and senior officers. The Administration's 2025 licensing guide still cites Order No. 412, item 409, as the approval basis and still cites the first captive notice for a change of name. The full texts and document numbers of the two captive notices were not on the Administration or State Council pages retrieved. The Administration's cleanup of 24 December 2025 did not list either notice among the normative documents it repealed or declared spent. The Insurance Law text published by the Administration sets capital in Article 69, preparation and opening periods in Articles 71 and 73, reporting in Article 86, and solvency supervision in Article 137. The 2019 related-party rules state that a captive's captive business is outside those rules. The 2019 corporate-governance assessment includes captive companies and says that separate rules on captive shareholders and governance prevail where they exist.

min_capital.Insurance Law floor: Registered capital of at least RMB 200 million (Insurance Law, Article 69). The supervisor may raise the floor for an insurer's business scope and scale and may not reduce it below RMB 200 million. Registered capital must be paid-in monetary capital. The Administration's 2023 licensing guide repeats that floor for the establishment of an insurance company and lists the Insurance Law among the conditions for a captive.
min_capital.Captive notices: The Administration's licensing guide treats two captive notices as additional conditions. Their full texts were not retrieved from a live Administration or State Council page. Any parent-company asset threshold, risk-matched capital formula, or other captive-specific amount in those notices is not restated.

tax_notes: Article 4 of the Enterprise Income Tax Law sets the enterprise income tax rate at 25 percent. The National People's Congress publishes that article, and the State Taxation Administration repeats it. The Administration states that a general taxpayer's value-added tax rate is 6 percent on financial services. The Foshan office of the Guangdong tax bureau, in its value-added-tax rate table for periods after 1 April 2019, lists insurance services at 6 percent. The Insurance Law text and the captive section of the licensing guide do not state a captive-specific income-tax or value-added-tax exemption. No premium-tax rate separate from value-added tax was stated on those pages.
contact_name: National Financial Regulatory Administration
types_allowed: Captive insurance companies approved by the National Financial Regulatory Administration under State Council Order No. 412, item 409
The four companies identified as captives on the Administration's legal-person list are classified on that list as property-insurance companies

fees.licensing_incorporation: No captive application fee or licence-issue fee was stated in the Administration's captive licensing guide or in the Insurance Law articles reviewed.
fees.annual_fees: No captive annual supervisory fee was stated in the Administration's captive licensing guide. The Administration's cleanup of 24 December 2025 declared spent the former notice that had temporarily suspended insurance regulatory fees. That cleanup does not publish a replacement fee amount.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Enterprise income tax of 25 percent under Article 4 of the Enterprise Income Tax Law. Value-added tax of 6 percent on insurance services for a general taxpayer. No separate premium-tax rate, and no captive-specific exemption from either tax, was stated in the Insurance Law text or the licensing guide.

annual_filing_requirements: Article 86 of the Insurance Law requires an insurance company to submit the reports, statements, documents and materials prescribed by the insurance supervisor. Solvency reports, financial accounting reports, actuarial reports, compliance reports and the other prescribed materials must record the insurance business truthfully. Article 137 requires the supervisor to establish a solvency supervision system and to monitor the solvency of insurance companies. The Administration's licensing guide lists the Insurance Law among the conditions for a captive and does not restate a captive-only filing calendar. Any quarterly captive report in the captive notices is not restated, because those notices were not retrieved from a live Administration or State Council page. The 2019 related-party measures state that they do not apply to a captive's captive business. The institution page publishes a petition-consultation telephone, 010-66279113, on working-day mornings and afternoons, and the banking and insurance consumer-complaint line 12378. It does not publish a general email address.

captive_administrator.name: National Financial Regulatory Administration

licensing_speed: State Council Order No. 412 states that procedures and time limits for the retained licensing items follow the Administrative License Law. Insurance Law Article 71 requires a decision on preparation of an insurance company within six months after acceptance. Article 73 requires a decision on opening within 60 days after acceptance of the opening application. The captive items in the Administration's 2023 licensing guide cite Order No. 412 and do not restate those Insurance Law periods as the captive timetable.

name: Connecticut
summary: Connecticut licenses captive insurance companies under Connecticut General Statutes sections 38a-91aa to 38a-91tt, enacted as Public Act 08-127 and effective 1 January 2009, and administered by the Captive Insurance Division of the Connecticut Insurance Department. The Division's formation page states that the law was amended in 2011, that the Division was established in 2012, and that the first two captives were licensed that year. A captive may be a pure, association, industrial insured, agency, sponsored, special purpose financial, or branch captive, or a risk retention group. A sponsored captive may also be licensed as a special purpose financial captive, and it may establish protected cells and incorporated protected cells. A parametric contract is permitted. A dormant captive, under section 38a-91uu, is a pure, sponsored, or industrial insured captive that has ceased transacting insurance business and has no insurance liabilities. Unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus is the greater of $50,000, or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary, for a pure captive; $75,000 on that basis for a sponsored captive; and $250,000 on that basis for an association, industrial insured, agency, or special purpose financial captive, and for a sponsored captive licensed as a special purpose financial captive. A risk retention group holds at least $1,000,000. A branch captive posts security of the greater of $50,000, or the amount the commissioner determines, plus reserves on branch business. The commissioner may allow any captive other than a risk retention group to hold less. A dormant captive maintains $15,000 and need not add capital on entering dormancy if it was never capitalized. Direct premium tax under section 38a-91nn is 0.380 percent, 0.285 percent, 0.190 percent, and 0.072 percent on successive $20 million bands. Assumed-reinsurance tax is 0.214 percent, 0.143 percent, 0.048 percent, and 0.024 percent. The annual minimum is $7,500 and the annual maximum is $200,000. A nonrefundable $7,500 credit applies in the first year tax is owed. The nonrefundable application fee is $800 and the initial and renewal license fee is $375. Bulletin FS-4C-25, dated 26 December 2025, requires the audited financial report five months after the fiscal year-end and directs filings to CID.CaptiveFilings@ct.gov. The Division pages name Fenhua Liu, Assistant Deputy Commissioner and Director of the Captive Division, and publish an individual mailbox for questions. They do not publish a captive census or a staff count. The application-materials page describes the review steps and does not state a single guaranteed licensing period.
legislation: Connecticut General Statutes sections 38a-91aa to 38a-91tt and 38a-91uu (Captive Insurance Companies), Public Act 08-127, effective 1 January 2009
applicable_legislation: Connecticut General Statutes sections 38a-91aa to 38a-91tt, originating in Public Act 08-127, effective 1 January 2009, and section 38a-91uu on dormant captives, added by Public Act 17-198. Capital and surplus are section 38a-91dd, revised by Public Act 22-118, effective 1 July 2022. The license and the $800 application fee are section 38a-91bb. The license fee amount is the captive insurance company license in section 38a-11, which the Department states as $375. Annual reports are section 38a-91gg. Examinations are section 38a-91hh, also revised by Public Act 22-118. Premium tax is section 38a-91nn. Protected cells are section 38a-91rr. The 2026 Supplement republishes amended sections 38a-91aa, 38a-91oo, 38a-91rr, and 38a-91zz. Dormancy tax relief was added by Public Act 23-15. Bulletin FS-4C-25 (26 December 2025) states the current financial-filing dates. The Department of Revenue Services captive-tax page, last reviewed 15 December 2025, states the return, the minimum, the maximum, and the dormant exemption.

min_capital.Pure captive: Not less than the greater of $50,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary for the company to meet its policy obligations (Conn. Gen. Stat. section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(A)). The Division's minimum-capital page states USD 50,000.
min_capital.Association captive: Not less than the greater of $250,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary (section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(B)).
min_capital.Industrial insured captive: Not less than the greater of $250,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary (section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(C)).
min_capital.Risk retention group: Not less than $1,000,000 (section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(D)). The discretion to allow less than the statutory floor does not apply to a risk retention group.
min_capital.Sponsored captive: Not less than the greater of $75,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary (section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(E)). The Division's minimum-capital page states USD 75,000 for the general account and states that the minimum capital for each cell depends on the risks taken. Section 38a-91dd does not state a separate dollar floor for a protected cell.
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: Not less than the greater of $250,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary (section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(F)).
min_capital.Sponsored captive licensed as a special: Not less than the greater of $250,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary (section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(G)).
min_capital.Agency captive: Not less than the greater of $250,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary (section 38a-91dd(a)(1)(H)).
min_capital.Branch captive: Security for branch liabilities of not less than the greater of $50,000 or an amount the commissioner determines is necessary, plus reserves on branch policies and reinsurance contracts, including losses, allocated loss-adjustment expenses, incurred-but-not-reported losses, and unearned premiums (section 38a-91dd(a)(2)). The commissioner may permit credit against those reserves for qualifying trust assets. The security may be a trust funded with acceptable assets, an irrevocable letter of credit from a bank the commissioner approves, cash on deposit with the commissioner for the base amount only, or a combination. The commissioner may exempt a foreign branch captive that the commissioner determines is financially stable.
min_capital.Dormant captive: Not less than $15,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus. A dormant captive that was never capitalized is not required to add capital on entering dormancy (section 38a-91uu(c)(1)). The Division's minimum-capital page states USD 15,000.
min_capital.Commissioner discretion and form of capi: The commissioner may allow a captive other than a risk retention group to maintain less than the subsection (a) floor, considering the type, volume, and nature of the business (section 38a-91dd(b)). Except for branch security, capital and surplus may be cash or an irrevocable letter of credit issued by a bank the commissioner approves (section 38a-91dd(c)). The commissioner may adopt regulations for additional capital and surplus (section 38a-91dd(d)).

tax_notes: Section 38a-91nn requires the tax by 1 March, paid to the Commissioner of Revenue Services. Direct premiums, after return premiums and policyholder dividends or premium deposits returned or credited, are taxed at 0.380 percent on the first $20 million, 0.285 percent on the next $20 million, 0.190 percent on the next $20 million, and 0.072 percent thereafter. Annuity considerations are not taxed. Assumed-reinsurance premiums are taxed at 0.214 percent, 0.143 percent, 0.048 percent, and 0.024 percent on those bands. Reinsurance tax does not apply to risks taxed on a direct basis, or to a qualifying assumption of loss reserves and other liabilities of another insurer under common ownership and control that is part of a plan to discontinue that insurer. For a captive other than a sponsored captive, the annual minimum aggregate tax is $7,500 and the annual maximum aggregate tax is $200,000. Branch tax applies only to branch business. For a sponsored captive, the $7,500 minimum applies to the company as a whole and not to each protected cell. Section 38a-91nn(c)(2) states that the annual maximum tax to be paid by a sponsored captive is the aggregate tax liability, calculated under the direct-premium subsection, of each protected cell. The Department of Revenue Services instructions, last reviewed 15 December 2025, state that the maximum aggregate tax to be paid by a sponsored captive applies to each protected cell and not to the sponsored captive as a whole. Two or more captives under common ownership and control are taxed as one captive. Common ownership and control is 80 percent of the voting stock, of the surplus and voting power of a mutual or nonprofit, or of the membership interests of a limited liability company. A protected cell is treated as a separate captive owned and controlled by its participants. A special purpose financial captive is not consolidated with a captive that is not a special purpose financial captive. The tax is all of the tax collectible under Connecticut law from a captive, and no other occupation tax is levied by the state or by a county, city, or municipality, except sales and use taxes and ad valorem taxes on real and personal property used to produce income. Multiyear premiums are prorated. A captive may claim a nonrefundable credit of $7,500 against the tax for the first calendar year on or after 1 January 2012 in which it has liability under the section. The Division's tax page shortens that credit to a $7,500 credit during the first year of operations. A dormant captive is not liable for the section 38a-91nn tax. The Department of Revenue Services states that the dormant exemption is effective 1 October 2023 and that a certificate of dormancy must be attached to the return. Form 207C is filed and paid on myconneCT by 1 March. A late payment draws the greater of 10 percent of the tax due or $50, plus interest of 1 percent per month or fraction of a month.
contact_name: Fenhua Liu, Assistant Deputy Commissioner and Director, Captive Insurance Division
types_allowed: Protected cells and incorporated protected cells
Special purpose financial captive insurance companies
Sponsored captives licensed as special purpose financial captives
Dormant captive insurance companies, limited to pure, sponsored, and industrial insured captives that hold a certificate of dormancy

fees.licensing_incorporation: Section 38a-91bb(d) requires a nonrefundable fee of $800 for examining, investigating, and processing the license application. The commissioner may retain outside legal, financial, and examination services and charge the reasonable cost to the company. The Division's premium-tax and fees page states the same one-time initial license application fee of $800. The license fee for the first year is the amount set in section 38a-11. The Division states that captive annual licensing fee as $375. Secretary of the State organization fees are not set in the captive sections.
fees.annual_fees: The license authorizes business until 1 April and may be renewed (section 38a-91bb(e)). The Division states the captive annual licensing fee as $375. The formation page states that the license renewal and fee are due on or before 1 March. A dormant captive pays the same captive license renewal fee (section 38a-91uu(c)(3)).
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums: 0.380 percent, 0.285 percent, 0.190 percent, and 0.072 percent on successive $20 million bands. Assumed reinsurance: 0.214 percent, 0.143 percent, 0.048 percent, and 0.024 percent on the same bands. Annual minimum $7,500. Annual maximum $200,000. For a sponsored captive the minimum applies to the company as a whole. The Department of Revenue Services states that the sponsored-captive maximum applies to each protected cell. Due 1 March on Form 207C. Nonrefundable $7,500 credit in the first year the tax is owed. A dormant captive pays no section 38a-91nn tax.

annual_filing_requirements: Section 38a-91gg requires a report of financial condition verified by the oath of two executive officers. The report is due before 1 March, and before 15 March for a pure captive or an industrial insured captive. Association captives and risk retention groups file in the form required by sections 38a-53 and 38a-53a. Reporting uses generally accepted accounting principles unless the commissioner requires, approves, or accepts statutory accounting principles or another comprehensive basis. A special purpose financial captive reports on statutory accounting principles unless the commissioner accepts another basis. A pure or industrial insured captive may be allowed to report on its fiscal year, with the report due not later than 75 days after fiscal year-end, and it still files calendar-year support before 15 March. A branch captive files copies of the reports required in the jurisdiction where the alien or foreign captive is formed, verified by two executive officers, on the domiciliary due date. The commissioner may waive the Connecticut annual report if those reports are adequate. A branch may be allowed to file 60 days after fiscal year-end. Bulletin FS-4C-25, dated 26 December 2025, states these due dates and adds an agency-captive due date of 1 March, with a permitted fiscal-year alternative of 75 days, and a dormant-captive due date of 15 March, with a permitted fiscal-year alternative of 75 days. The bulletin requires a statement of opinion on loss and loss-adjustment-expense reserves by a member of the American Academy of Actuaries or a qualified loss-reserve specialist. Under sections 38a-54 and 38a-91oo, each captive except a dormant captive files a financial report certified by an independent public accountant. The bulletin states that the audited report is due annually five months after the end of the fiscal accounting period. Premium tax on Form 207C is due 1 March. Filings are submitted to CID.CaptiveFilings@ct.gov. Applications for deviations and requests for waivers go to CID.CaptiveRequests@ct.gov. The board of directors, the committee of managers, or a reciprocal's subscribers' advisory committee meets at least once each year in Connecticut. The principal place of business is in Connecticut, and a registered agent is appointed. The formation page also states that one board member and a licensed agent must be Connecticut residents and that accounts are established with a bank in Connecticut. Section 38a-91hh requires an examination whenever the commissioner determines it to be prudent, and not less frequently than once every five years. The commissioner may waive that examination for a pure captive or for a branch captive of a pure captive. The examination is at the company's cost, with the salary limitation stated in the section. The formation page still describes an examination every three years that may be extended to five. That page predates the Public Act 22-118 revision of section 38a-91hh, and the current statute is followed here. A dormant captive files the 15 March financial-condition report and pays the renewal fee. The certificate of dormancy is renewed once every five years and is forfeited if insurance business resumes or the certificate is not timely renewed.

captive_administrator.name: Fenhua Liu, Assistant Deputy Commissioner and Director, Captive Insurance Division, Connecticut Insurance Department

licensing_speed: The application-and-regulatory-materials page states that, within the first two business days after filing, the Department assigns an analyst; that the analyst reviews completeness within two business days; that the financial, operational, and risk-profile review is expected to take up to five business days, depending on the risk profile and complexity; that a peer or supervisory review, when needed, is completed within five business days; and that notice of approval or denial is issued immediately after the final supervisory review. The page does not state a single guaranteed number of days from a complete filing to a license. The statute does not state a licensing-day standard. The license, once granted, authorizes business until 1 April.
