name: Cook Islands
summary: The Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission licenses captive insurers under the Captive Insurance Act 2013. The Captive Insurance (Commencement) Order 2013, the first instrument in the Commission's regulations file, deems the Act to have come into force on 11 June 2013. The Act applies to an international company carrying on captive insurance business outside the Cook Islands, and to a company incorporated under the Companies Act that insures only the interests of its holding company, that holding company also being incorporated under the Companies Act. Captive insurance business is the business of insuring interests in the insurer's holding company, or in companies with which it is affiliated or associated, or with which it is organised in a group or agency relationship. Regulation 5 sets the prescribed minimum capital and surplus at $100,000. Section 3 of the Act defines a dollar as the New Zealand dollar unless another currency is expressly provided, and the regulations adopt the Act's definitions. The Commission may direct a higher amount or allow a lower amount. The Captive Insurance Amendment Regulations 2014, deemed in force on 1 May 2014, set an application fee of $1,100, a licence fee of $3,100, and an annual renewal fee of $3,100 for a licensed captive insurer. The Commission's prescribed-fees page says Commission fees are denominated in United States dollars except where otherwise stated. The fee schedule itself does not say United States dollars. An application is made through a Cook Islands trustee company or an approved insurance manager, and regulation 9 says the Commission will determine the application within 60 days of receipt. A licensed captive insurer has at least two directors, at least one of them a natural person resident in the Cook Islands, and appoints an approved insurance manager and an auditor. Signed financial statements and the auditor's report are due within five months of financial year-end. The Captive Insurance Amendment Act 2019, No. 13, assented to on 17 December 2019 and in force on 18 December 2019, repealed section 48, which had shielded an international-company captive from Cook Islands tax. The Commission does not publish a captive census or a staff count on the pages reviewed. The contact page publishes the generic inbox Inquire@fsc.gov.ck. It states that the office line +682 20798 is currently down and gives named mobiles for urgent calls. Those personal numbers are not recorded here.
legislation: Captive Insurance Act 2013, as amended by the Captive Insurance Amendment Act 2019, and the Captive Insurance Regulations 2013, as amended by the Captive Insurance Amendment Regulations 2014
applicable_legislation: Captive Insurance Act 2013. The Captive Insurance (Commencement) Order 2013 deems the Act to have come into force on 11 June 2013. The scope is section 4 and the definition of captive insurance business is section 3. Capital and surplus are section 12, and the prescribed minimum is regulation 5 of the Captive Insurance Regulations 2013. Directors are section 15. The approved insurance manager is section 17. The auditor is section 19. Returns are section 23, and the five-month filing rule is regulation 14. Fees are section 42 and Schedule 2 as substituted by the Captive Insurance Amendment Regulations 2014, deemed to have come into force on 1 May 2014. The 60-day determination is regulation 9. The Captive Insurance Amendment Act 2019, No. 13, was assented to on 17 December 2019, came into force the next day, and repealed section 48. For an international company, the International Companies (Removal of Tax Exemption) Amendment Act 2019, No. 12, also assented to on 17 December 2019, replaced section 249 of the International Companies Act 1981-82. The International Companies (Removal of Tax Exemption) Transitional Provisions Regulations 2021, made on 1 June 2021 and deemed in force on 18 December 2019, modify that transitional rule until the close of 31 December 2021. Company tax is the Income Tax Act 1997, First Schedule, in the text published by the Ministry of Finance and Economic Management.

min_capital.Prescribed minimum: Regulation 5 sets the prescribed minimum capital and surplus of a licensed captive insurer at $100,000. Section 12 requires capital and surplus of at least the higher of that prescribed minimum and any higher amount the Commission directs. The Commission may allow an amount below the prescribed minimum and may later direct an increase. Section 3 defines dollar, and the $ sign, as the New Zealand dollar unless another meaning is expressly provided. Regulation 4 gives Act definitions the same meaning in the regulations. The regulations do not state a different currency.
min_capital.What counts as capital and surplus: Section 3 defines capital as fully paid-up share capital. Surplus is the amount by which assets exceed liabilities. Regulation 5 says only Schedule 1 admissible assets count, assets are valued under regulation 6 and not above market value, and liabilities are valued under regulation 7, including contingent and prospective liabilities. Admissible assets include advances to the holding company at a market interest rate, cash with an approved financial institution, an irrevocable letter of credit from an approved financial institution, approved government-guaranteed bonds, quoted securities up to 70 percent of quoted market value, premiums receivable, reinsurance balances receivable, and accounts receivable net of a provision for doubtful debts.
min_capital.One floor for every licensed captive: The Act and the regulations do not set a separate dollar floor for a holding-company, group, association, or agency programme. The same prescribed minimum applies to every licensed captive insurer. The Commission may direct more, or allow less, having regard to the nature and extent of the business.

tax_notes: The Captive Insurance Act does not impose a premium tax. Section 48, before its repeal, provided that no Cook Islands Act could impose a tax, levy, or duty on a licensed captive insurer incorporated under the International Companies Act, other than the statutes listed in that section. The Income Tax Act was not in that list. The Captive Insurance Amendment Act 2019 repealed section 48. It was assented to on 17 December 2019 and came into force on 18 December 2019. For an international company, the International Companies (Removal of Tax Exemption) Amendment Act 2019 replaced section 249 so that the Income Tax Act 1997 and the Value Added Tax Act 1997 are among the Acts that may impose obligations. An international company incorporated on or after 18 December 2019 is within the amended provisions immediately. For a company incorporated before that date, the former sections 243, 249, and 250 continued until the close of 31 December 2021, and the amended sections 243 and 249 apply to all international companies on and after 1 January 2022. The transitional regulations, which ceased to apply at the close of 31 December 2021, also brought new intellectual-property income and new revenue-generating activities within the amended Act from 18 December 2019. The Income Tax Act text published by the Ministry of Finance and Economic Management states, in First Schedule clause 3, a basic company rate of 20 cents for every $1 for each income year after the income year commencing on 1 January 1997. The resident and non-resident split in clause 3(a), 20 cents and 24 cents, is stated only for that 1997 income year. Clause 2 states a rate of 3 cents for every $1 on income assessable to an overseas insurance company under sections 74 and 140. That clause was not identified as the rate for a captive licensed under the Captive Insurance Act. Later amending Acts were not separately retrieved, so the rate stated here is the rate in the Act text the Ministry publishes. No captive premium-tax rate was found in the captive legislation. The Value Added Tax Act 1997 may apply to an international company under section 249 as replaced. A value-added-tax rate for a captive was not stated in the captive legislation or in that Income Tax Act text.
contact_name: Financial Supervisory Commission
types_allowed: International companies licensed to carry on captive insurance business outside the Cook Islands
Companies incorporated under the Companies Act that insure only the interests of their holding companies, those holding companies also being incorporated under the Companies Act
Captive insurance business covering a holding company, an affiliated or associated company, or a company organised with the insurer in a group or agency relationship

fees.licensing_incorporation: Schedule 2, as substituted by the Captive Insurance Amendment Regulations 2014 and deemed in force on 1 May 2014, charges a licensed captive insurer an application fee of $1,100 and a licence fee of $3,100. An external insurance manager pays an application fee of $400 and a licence fee of $400. The licence fee in the first year is paid on a pro rata basis up to 30 June. Section 3 of the Act defines dollar as the New Zealand dollar unless expressly provided otherwise, and the schedule does not state another currency. The Commission's prescribed-fees page says fees are denominated in United States dollars except where otherwise stated. Incorporation fees of the registry are not set in Schedule 2.
fees.annual_fees: The annual renewal fee is $3,100 for a licensed captive insurer and $400 for an external insurance manager, payable on 1 July. After the first year the licence fee is paid in full on 1 July. Section 42(5) says that if the annual fee is not paid within 90 days of the due date, the Commission may require the licensee to surrender its licence. The same currency point applies: the schedule uses the Act's dollar, and the prescribed-fees page describes Commission fees as United States dollars except where otherwise stated.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the Captive Insurance Act or the regulations. The Income Tax Act text published by the Ministry states a company rate of 20 cents for every $1 for income years after the 1997 income year. Later amending Acts were not separately retrieved.

annual_filing_requirements: Regulation 14 requires the financial statements, signed by at least one director after approval by the directors, to be submitted within five months of the financial year-end, or within an extension the Commission allows. They are accompanied by a directors' certificate in the approved form and the auditor's report. The statements give a true and fair view and comply with International Financial Reporting Standards, New Zealand Generally Accepted Accounting Practice, or another international standard the Commission approves. The financial year runs to the quarter-end anniversary of incorporation unless the Commission allows the group year or another date. Section 19 requires an auditor approved by the Commission, independent of the insurer, and section 20 requires an audit report in compliance with the regulations. Section 15 requires at least two directors, at least one a natural person residing in the Cook Islands, and prior written approval before a director is appointed. A termination is notified within 14 days. Section 17 requires an approved insurance manager at all times, either an insurance manager licensed under the Insurance Act or an external insurance manager approved under the Act. That approval is reviewed annually. Section 18 requires records sufficient to explain the transactions and to prepare the required statements. The resident director must be able to access them. The Act provides for compliance visits and for appointment of an examiner. It does not state a fixed examination interval in the sections reviewed. The annual fee is due on 1 July. The contact page publishes Inquire@fsc.gov.ck and postal address PO Box 594, Avarua, Rarotonga. It states that the office telephone +682 20798 is currently down.

captive_administrator.name: Financial Supervisory Commission

licensing_speed: Regulation 9(3) of the Captive Insurance Regulations 2013 says the Commission will make a determination on an application for a licence within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application. Section 9 of the Act requires the Commission to issue the licence, issue it subject to conditions, or refuse the application. The licence remains valid until revoked, subject to section 29.

name: Delaware
summary: Delaware licenses captives under Title 18, Chapter 69 of the Delaware Code. The Department of Insurance Bureau of Captive and Financial Insurance Products administers the chapter, and the Bureau's welcome page identifies House Bill 218 (2005) as the statute that modernized the law. The Department's 2025 year-in-review reported 638 captives after 51 new licences that year. Minimum capital and surplus is $250,000 for a pure, agency, branch or special purpose captive, $500,000 for an industrial insured captive or a sponsored captive, $750,000 for an association captive, and $1,000,000 for a risk retention group. A series captive's minimum is the amount the Commissioner specifies. Direct premium tax is 0.2 percent, with a $200,000 direct-tax cap, and assumed reinsurance premium tax is 0.1 percent, with a $110,000 cap. The annual minimum is $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive, and the annual aggregate cap is $200,000. Under § 6914(d) that premium tax is in lieu of other Delaware state and local occupation taxes, other than ad valorem property tax. A conditional certificate of authority is dated the day the Bureau receives the emailed application, if the $3,600 fee arrives within 10 business days.
legislation: Title 18, Delaware Code, Chapter 69 (Captive Insurance Companies); the Bureau identifies House Bill 218 (2005) as the modernizing statute
applicable_legislation: Title 18, Delaware Code, Chapter 69 (Captive Insurance Companies), including § 6902 (definitions), § 6903 (licence application, fees and conditional certificates), § 6905 (minimum capital and surplus), § 6906 (formation), § 6907 (annual reports), § 6914 (tax on premiums) and § 6924 (dormant captive insurance companies). The current text is published on the Delaware Code Online.

min_capital.Branch captive: USD $250,000, or such other amount as the Commissioner determines (§ 6905(a)(8))
min_capital.Special purpose captive: USD $250,000, or such other amount as the Commissioner determines (§ 6905(a)(7))
min_capital.Sponsored captive: USD $500,000 (§ 6905(a)(6)). This is the sponsored captive minimum, not a published per-cell floor
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: USD $500,000 if it is also a sponsored captive; USD $250,000 if it is not (§ 6905(a)(9))
min_capital.Series captive: The amount specified by the Commissioner (§ 6905(a)(10)). No default dollar amount is published in the statute
min_capital.Additional and form of capital: The Commissioner may prescribe additional capital and surplus based on the type, volume and nature of the business (§ 6905(b)). Minimum capital is held as cash, an irrevocable letter of credit from an institution chartered, licensed or otherwise authorized to do banking business in Delaware, or another institution or asset the Commissioner approves. Surplus-note proceeds may count if the Commissioner approves the note (§ 6905(c) and (d))

tax_notes: Direct premiums are taxed at 2/10 of 1 percent (0.2 percent), up to $200,000, and assumed reinsurance premiums at 1/10 of 1 percent (0.1 percent), up to $110,000. Premiums already taxed as direct premiums are not taxed again as assumed reinsurance, and no tax is due on annuity consideration. The annual minimum aggregate tax is $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive. The annual maximum aggregate tax is $200,000, except that series captives formed in the same limited liability company or statutory trust are not aggregated into that cap. A captive that employs at least 25 qualified full-time individuals in Delaware pays $50,000 if the formula would otherwise exceed that amount. Tax is due by 15 April. Under § 6914(d) this premium tax is all of the tax collectible under Delaware law from a captive, and no other occupation tax is levied by the State or by a county, city or municipality, except ad valorem taxes on real and personal property used in the production of income. A dormant captive is not liable for the premium tax. There is no separate Delaware corporate income tax on captives in Chapter 69.
contact_name: Stephen Taylor, Director, Bureau of Captive & Financial Insurance Products

fees.licensing_incorporation: Nonrefundable application fee of $300 to review completeness, plus a nonrefundable processing fee of $3,200 (18 Del. C. § 6903(d)). The 2024 Bureau application notice collects $3,500 for a regular application. A conditional certificate adds a $100 fee under § 6903(d)(5); the same 2024 notice collects $3,600 for a conditional application. The annual licence fee for the year of registration is $400.
fees.annual_fees: $400 certificate-of-authority renewal fee, due 15 April, payable with the premium-tax report. From the 2025 premium tax and 2026 renewal, payment may be made through OPTins or by the existing procedure. A dormant captive that has not resumed business after five years pays a renewal fee of $25,000 in the sixth year of dormancy and $5,000 in each year of dormancy after that (§ 6924(g)).
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums 0.2 percent, maximum $200,000. Assumed reinsurance premiums 0.1 percent, maximum $110,000. Annual minimum aggregate tax $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive. Annual maximum aggregate tax $200,000. A captive with at least 25 qualified Delaware employees is capped at $50,000. No annuity tax. Dormant captives pay no premium tax.

annual_filing_requirements: Each captive other than a branch captive for which the Commissioner has waived the requirement files a report of financial condition by 15 April, verified by oath of two executive officers or authorized persons, using GAAP unless the Commissioner approves statutory accounting principles or international accounting standards (§ 6907). The Bureau requires the annual report (Form F-1, updated 31 March 2025, for pure captives, core LLCs and series; special purpose financial captives that file NAIC statements are excepted) by 15 April, or within 60 days of fiscal year-end where an alternate year-end is used. Audited financial statements and a statement of actuarial opinion, for captives that retain risk, are due by 30 June. Special purpose financial captives also file quarterly reports with the NAIC and the Bureau by 15 May, 15 August and 15 November. Premium tax and the $400 renewal fee are due by 15 April. Annual reports are emailed to captive@delaware.gov.

captive_administrator.name: Stephen Taylor, Director, Bureau of Captive & Financial Insurance Products, Delaware Department of Insurance

licensing_speed: The 2024 Bureau application notice dates a conditional certificate on the day the emailed application is received, provided the $3,600 fee reaches the Dover accounting office within 10 business days. Only a captive manager that already manages at least two Delaware captives may file a conditional application. In October 2023 the Department said its goal for review of initial application filings is 30 days, down from 45, and that conditional applications received after 1 November are reviewed within 80 days. That 2023 goal is not restated in the 2024 notice or the March 2026 OPTins notice.

name: District of Columbia
summary: The District of Columbia licenses captives under the Captive Insurance Company Act of 2004, Chapter 39A of Title 31 of the D.C. Code, administered by the Department of Insurance, Securities and Banking Risk Finance Bureau. The 2000 captive law was repealed and replaced by that Act. The first captive was licensed in 2001. A captive may be a pure, association, agency, rental, branch, or protected-cell captive, and a risk retention group may be licensed as a captive. Any type of captive may form protected cells, including incorporated cells that are separate legal entities. Special purpose financial captives are authorized in Subchapter II. A wildcard provision lets the Commissioner authorize a qualified captive to engage in any activity permitted for a captive in any other jurisdiction. On 30 October 2025 the Bureau reported 215 active risk-bearing entities: 49 pure, including 6 protected-cell-captive cores; 10 association captives that are not risk retention groups, including 3 protected-cell-captive cores; 1 agency protected-cell captive; 4 branch captives; 16 rental captives, all protected-cell captives; 29 risk retention groups; and 106 protected cells, of which 78 were unincorporated and 28 were incorporated. Through that date in 2025 the Bureau had licensed 23 entities: 1 incorporated cell, 20 unincorporated protected cells, and 2 risk retention groups. It also said 413 captives had been licensed since 2001. The same presentation reported 2024 captive assets of $11,396,881,785 and 2024 gross written premium of $2,954,868,515. DISB also posts a licensed-captives roster dated 14 July 2026. That roster does not state a total, so the 30 October 2025 census is the figure stored here. A captive other than a protected-cell captive maintains at least $100,000 of unimpaired capital. Unencumbered surplus is at least $150,000 for a pure captive, $300,000 for an agency captive, a rental captive, or a stock association captive, and $500,000 for a mutual or reciprocal association captive. The Commissioner sets cell capital and surplus, and the Bureau's 30 October 2025 presentation states that the minimum is $0 for a protected-cell captive and $0 for cells, including incorporated cells. Non-risk-retention-group direct premium tax starts at 0.25 percent on the first $25 million, with a $7,500 minimum and a $100,000 maximum. The application review fee is $500 and the certificate-of-authority fee is $300, renewed annually by 30 April. Properly documented applications are processed within 30 days. The Bureau page still displays Dana Sheppard as Associate Commissioner for Risk Finance. The 30 October 2025 presentation lists her as Deputy Commissioner for Market Operations and lists Sean O'Donnell as Associate Commissioner, and the Bureau's 7 November 2025 and 17 December 2025 notices are issued by Sean O'Donnell in that office. No dormant-captive statute is in force. The October 2025 presentation said a proposal to add one had been submitted and that no significant captive law had passed in 2025.
legislation: Captive Insurance Company Act of 2004, D.C. Code Title 31, Chapter 39A
applicable_legislation: D.C. Code Title 31, Chapter 39A, Subchapter I, enacted as D.C. Law 15-262 (17 March 2005) and amended since, including the Captive Insurance Company Amendment Act of 2014, D.C. Law 20-203. Chapter 39, the 2000 captive law, is repealed by section 31-3931.23. Capital and surplus are section 31-3931.06. Protected cells are section 31-3931.04. Premium tax is section 31-3931.12. The annual report is section 31-3931.13. Financial examination is section 31-3931.14. Certificate-of-authority renewal by 30 April is section 31-3931.09(d), as cited in the Bureau's 2025 reporting instructions. Special purpose financial captive capital is section 31-3932.05. Non-risk-retention-group audit timing is also in 26 DCMR section 3702, as cited by the Bureau.

min_capital.Captive other than a protected cell capt: At least $100,000 of minimum unimpaired capital, in addition to any further capital the Commissioner requires (D.C. Code section 31-3931.06(a)(1)).
min_capital.Pure captive: At least $150,000 of unencumbered surplus, in addition to required capital (section 31-3931.06(f)(1)).
min_capital.Protected cell captive and each protecte: The Commissioner sets the minimum capital and the minimum surplus for the protected cell captive and for each cell. Protected-cell-captive capital may be zero if each cell maintains the capital required for that cell. A protected cell captive that does not write insurance business in the District is not required to maintain surplus if each cell maintains the surplus required for that cell (section 31-3931.06(a)(2) and (f)(6)). The Bureau's 30 October 2025 presentation states the minimum as $0 for protected cell captives and $0 for cells, including incorporated cells.
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: At least $100,000 of unimpaired capital and at least $150,000 of unencumbered surplus (section 31-3932.05(a) and (e)).
min_capital.Risk retention group: Section 31-3931.06(l) applies section 31-2502.12 to a risk retention group licensed as a captive. The captive surplus schedule does not state a separate risk-retention-group dollar floor, and no separate floor is restated here.
min_capital.Form of capital and surplus: Cash or an irrevocable letter of credit, unless the Commissioner provides otherwise. The letter of credit is issued by a District-chartered bank, or a District branch of a Federal Reserve member bank or an FDIC-insured bank, on a form the Commissioner approves, and it renews automatically each year.

tax_notes: Section 31-3931.12 requires premium tax by 2 March. For a captive that is not a risk retention group, net direct premiums are taxed at 0.250 percent on the first $25 million, 0.150 percent on the next $25 million, and 0.050 percent thereafter. A risk retention group pays 0.38 percent on the first $20 million of total net direct premiums, 0.25 percent on the next $20 million, and 0.18 percent thereafter. Assumed-reinsurance premiums are taxed at 0.225 percent on the first $25 million, 0.150 percent on the next $25 million, and 0.025 percent thereafter. Reinsurance tax is not levied on risks already taxed as direct premiums, or on a qualifying assumption of loss reserves from an insurer under common ownership and control that is being discontinued. A captive other than a risk retention group licensed as an association captive pays at least $7,500. A risk retention group licensed as an association captive pays at least $15,000. The total tax does not exceed $100,000 in any year. Annuity business is not taxed. Branch tax applies only to branch business. A captive licensed in the last quarter of the calendar year may ask the Commissioner to reduce the minimum. The tax is in lieu of other District taxes except real property tax and personal property tax. The Bureau's 2025 reporting instructions say each protected cell captive and each incorporated cell files a separate premium-tax return, incorporated cells are subject to the $7,500 minimum, unincorporated protected cells file a consolidated return with the protected cell captive, and each unincorporated protected cell is not subject to the minimum. From 1 January 2026, premium tax and certificate-of-authority renewal payments are made through NAIC OPTins. The NAIC charges $17.50 per OPTins transaction.
contact_name: Sean O'Donnell, Associate Commissioner, Risk Finance Bureau
types_allowed: Incorporated protected cells and unincorporated protected cells
Risk retention groups licensed as captive insurers
Special purpose financial captive insurance companies

fees.licensing_incorporation: The forming page and the Bureau's 30 October 2025 presentation require a $500 application review fee and a $300 certificate-of-authority fee with the application. Incorporation is handled inside the Department. The presentation states that there are no fees other than the $500 application fee, the $300 annual certificate-of-authority fee, and annual premium taxes. Section 31-3931.04(b)(4) also says a protected cell captive pays an additional annual fee for each protected cell in an amount the Commissioner establishes. No separate dollar amount for that cell fee was published on the pages reviewed. A certification of captive documents is $10, paid in advance, under the Bureau's certification-fee notice.
fees.annual_fees: Annual certificate-of-authority renewal fee of $300, due on or before 30 April under section 31-3931.09(d), as stated in the 17 December 2025 reporting instructions. Beginning with the 2026-2027 renewals, renewal payments are made through NAIC OPTins. The NAIC charges $17.50 per transaction. The Commissioner may fine, suspend, or revoke a certificate that is not renewed by 1 August.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Non-risk-retention-group direct premiums: 0.25 percent on the first $25 million, 0.15 percent on the next $25 million, and 0.05 percent thereafter. Risk-retention-group direct premiums: 0.38 percent, 0.25 percent, and 0.18 percent on successive $20 million bands. Assumed reinsurance: 0.225 percent, 0.150 percent, and 0.025 percent on successive $25 million bands. Minimum $7,500, or $15,000 for a risk retention group licensed as an association captive. Maximum $100,000. Due 2 March. Incorporated cells owe the $7,500 minimum. An unincorporated protected cell is not separately subject to the minimum.

annual_filing_requirements: On or before 2 March, a captive, including each protected cell, submits a report of its financial condition prepared by a certified public accountant. Reporting uses generally accepted accounting principles unless the Commissioner accepts modifications. A protected cell captive files a consolidated report for its cells, and the 2025 instructions also require separate unaudited DC blanks for the protected cell captive, each incorporated cell, and each unincorporated protected cell. A pure captive may be allowed to report on its parent's fiscal year, with the report due within 60 days after fiscal year-end, and it still files premium-tax support by 2 March. Risk retention groups also comply with Chapter 3 of Title 31 and file the actuarial opinion by 2 March and the actuarial opinion summary by 15 March. Non-risk-retention-group audited financial reports are due 30 June under 26 DCMR section 3702. Risk-retention-group audits are due 1 June. Combined cell audits and combined actuarial opinions, when used, are due 30 June. A branch captive files copies of the reports its parent files at home, certified by two officers, plus a branch premium and reserve statement. For a 31 December branch, those filings are due 30 June. Premium tax is due 2 March. The certificate of authority is renewed by 30 April. Financial filings are emailed to captive.filings@dc.gov. From 1 January 2026, premium tax and renewal payments go through OPTins. The board meets at least once each year in the District. The Bureau's one-pager states that the meeting may be held by teleconference or webcast and that a local director is not required. The captive maintains an office in the District. Examinations are at the Commissioner's discretion and at the captive's cost. The Commissioner may waive the five-year examination in Chapter 14 for a captive that is not a risk retention group, has filed unqualified audits, has sufficient surplus, and is in compliance. The 30 October 2025 presentation describes non-risk-retention-group supervision as an annual desk analysis, with examinations at the regulator's discretion. No dormant-captive filing regime is in the current statute.

captive_administrator.name: Sean O'Donnell, Associate Commissioner, Risk Finance Bureau

licensing_speed: DISB will process a properly documented application within 30 days. The forming page states that standard, and the Bureau's 30 October 2025 presentation states licensing of 30 days or less. The one-pager also states that many business-plan changes are approved within 48 hours.

name: Dubai
summary: Dubai's captive regime is the Dubai International Financial Centre regime administered by the Dubai Financial Services Authority. A captive insurer is a Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3 captive insurer, and each class is a DIFC-incorporated insurer. A Class 1 captive may insure only risks related to or arising out of the business or operations of its group, including reinsurance of those risks. A Class 2 captive must obtain at least 51 percent of gross written premium in any year from group risks, and the remainder from persons who do business with the group through related or common businesses, activities, trade, services, or operations. A Class 3 captive insures only persons engaged in similar, related, or common businesses, activities, trade, services, or operations, and it is owned by those persons or by a body corporate of which all of them are members. The same three classes exist as cells of a protected cell company. PIN Rule A4.2.3 requires minimum capital of at least $150,000 for Class 1, $500,000 for Class 2, and $1,000,000 for Class 3. The Class 1 minimum capital requirement is the higher of the underwriting risk component and the reserving risk component. Class 2 and Class 3 add the default risk and investment volatility risk components. For a captive, the underwriting component uses net written premium. The Fees Module in force as FER/VER35/04-26 states an application fee of $5,500 to effect or carry out contracts of insurance as a captive insurer or as an insurance special purpose vehicle, and the same figure is the captive line in the annual-fee table. A protected cell company is charged $8,000 for the core and $1,000 for each cell, and the applicant pays the highest applicable fee. The annual fee also includes an expenditure component calculated from the PIN return and can include a 100 percent loading if the insurer is part of a Financial Stability Board global systemically important group or if the DFSA is consolidated or lead supervisor. The DFSA insurance summary says UAE Federal Law No. 8 of 2004 requires insurers in the DIFC to conduct reinsurance only for risks situated in the UAE, while direct insurance may cover risks situated in the DIFC and risks situated offshore of the UAE. The text of that federal law was not retrieved. The DFSA does not publish a captive census, a staff count, or a licensing-day standard on the pages reviewed. The contact page publishes the telephone and the office address and directs enquiries to an online form. A DFSA publication on the same website, last modified in March 2024, lists general enquiries at info@dfsa.ae.
legislation: DFSA Rulebook Glossary Module (GLO) VER66/07-26, Prudential — Insurance Business Module (PIN), and Fees Module (FER) VER35/04-26
applicable_legislation: Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3 captive insurers, and the matching captive cells, are defined in the Glossary Module. The Class 1 definition derives from DFSA RM12/2004, made on 16 September 2004, as amended from 15 October 2004. The Class 2 and Class 3 definitions were added by RM14/2004 from 15 October 2004. Class 2 was amended by RM295/2021, made on 24 February 2021. The minimum capital requirement formula is PIN Rule A4.2.1 and the dollar floors are PIN Rule A4.2.3, amended by RMI296/2021, made on 24 February 2021. A higher Class 2 floor, which must remain below $1,000,000, is PIN Rule A4.2.4. Captive base premium is net written premium under PIN Rule A4.10.6. The annual regulatory return is due within four months under PIN Rule 6.5.1, amended by RMI350/2023, made on 22 February 2023. The quarterly exemption for a Class 1 captive and for a protected cell company whose cells are all Class 1 or Class 2 captive cells is PIN Rule 6.3.4. Fees are the Fees Module FER/VER35/04-26, Rules 1.2, 2.1.1, 3.1.1, and 3.2. UAE corporate tax is Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022. Qualifying activities and excluded activities for a Qualifying Free Zone Person are Ministerial Decision No. 229 of 2025.

min_capital.How the minimum is set: PIN Rule A4.2.1 calculates the minimum capital requirement for a Class 1 captive insurer as the higher of the underwriting risk component and the reserving risk component. For a Class 2 or Class 3 captive insurer it is the sum of the default risk component, the investment volatility risk component, the underwriting risk component, and the reserving risk component. PIN Rule A4.2.3 requires that result to be at least $150,000 for Class 1, $500,000 for Class 2, and $1,000,000 for Class 3. A non-captive insurer's floor in the same rule is $10,000,000. The component formulas other than the captive premium base and the reserving percentages were not restated.
min_capital.Class 1 captive insurer: At least $150,000 (PIN Rule A4.2.3(a)). The insurer is a DIFC-incorporated insurer permitted to effect or carry out contracts of insurance only for risks related to or arising out of the business or operations of the group, including reinsurance of those risks.
min_capital.Class 2 captive insurer: At least $500,000, or a higher amount the DFSA specifies in writing under PIN Rule A4.2.4. Any higher amount must be less than $1,000,000. The licence conditions require at least 51 percent of gross written premium in any year from group risks. The remainder must come from persons who engage by way of business in commercial activities with the group through related or common businesses, activities, trade, services, or operations, including reinsurance of those risks.
min_capital.Class 3 captive insurer: At least $1,000,000 (PIN Rule A4.2.3(c)). The insurer may cover only risks of persons engaged in similar, related, or common businesses, activities, trade, services, or operations, including reinsurance of those risks, and it is owned by those persons or by a body corporate of which all of them are members.
min_capital.Underwriting and reserving components: PIN Rule A4.10.6(b) sets a captive insurer's base premium at its net written premium for the reference period. Net written premium is gross written premium less premium on reinsurance contracts the insurer enters as cedant. A non-captive uses the higher of net written premium and 50 percent of gross written premium. The class percentages applied to base premium are in PIN Rule A4.10.1 and were not copied here. PIN Rule A4.11.1 sets the reserving risk component by multiplying the base claims reserve by a class factor. The factors in that table, for direct insurance, proportional reinsurance, and non-proportional and facultative reinsurance alike, are 28 for classes 1 and 2, 12 for class 3, 16 for class 4, 22 for class 5, 10 for class 6, 31.25 for classes 7(a) and 7(b), and 28 for class 8.
min_capital.Cells and insurance special purpose vehi: A protected cell company may establish a Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3 captive cell on the same risk limits as the matching captive insurer. The Glossary does not state a separate cell dollar floor in the definitions reviewed. An insurance special purpose vehicle is an insurer defined separately from the three captive classes. Its fee line is paired with the captive fee. Its capital floor is the non-captive calculation unless a captive definition applies, and no separate ISPV dollar floor was extracted.

tax_notes: The Fees Module does not impose a premium tax. UAE corporate tax is Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022. A Qualifying Free Zone Person pays 0 percent on Qualifying Income and 9 percent on taxable income that is not Qualifying Income. The Federal Tax Authority's free-zone bulletin states that a Qualifying Free Zone Person is not eligible for the 0 percent rate on the first AED 375,000 and pays 9 percent on its entire taxable income that is not Qualifying Income. Ministerial Decision No. 229 of 2025 lists reinsurance services as a Qualifying Activity. It lists insurance activities, defined as insurance operations regulated under Federal Decree-Law No. 48 of 2023, as an Excluded Activity, without prejudice to reinsurance services and to headquarter services to Related Parties. Income from an Excluded Activity is not eligible for the 0 percent rate. Whether a particular DIFC captive is a Qualifying Free Zone Person, and whether a particular contract is reinsurance, headquarter services, or an excluded insurance activity, is determined under those federal instruments and is not set by a captive class in the DFSA Rulebook. The DFSA modules reviewed do not state a corporate-tax holiday to 2054, and that date is not used here. No captive-specific value-added-tax rate is stated in the modules reviewed.
contact_name: Dubai Financial Services Authority
types_allowed: Class 1 captive insurers, limited to group risks, including reinsurance of those risks
Class 2 captive insurers, with at least 51 percent of gross written premium from group risks and the remainder from related commercial counterparties
Class 3 captive insurers, owned by persons in a similar, related, or common business
Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3 captive cells of a protected cell company
Insurance special purpose vehicles, authorised separately from the three captive classes

fees.licensing_incorporation: FER Rule 2.1.1, in FER/VER35/04-26, charges $5,500 to apply for a licence to effect or carry out contracts of insurance as a captive insurer or as an insurance special purpose vehicle. A protected cell company pays $8,000 for the core and $1,000 for each cell. The applicant pays the highest of the applicable fees in the table, plus an additional 100 percent of that fee if any complexity factor in Rule 2.1.1(3) applies, including a group incorporated in two or more jurisdictions outside the DIFC, a holding company in the DIFC, a jurisdiction with no bilateral memorandum of understanding, or the DFSA acting as consolidated or lead supervisor. The application is not regarded as submitted until the fee is paid in full. DIFC commercial-licence fees are not set in the captive rows.
fees.annual_fees: The captive or insurance special purpose vehicle line in the Rule 3.2.1 table is $5,500. The protected cell company line is $8,000 for the core and $1,000 for each cell. The annual fee is the highest applicable line, plus any Rule 3.2.3 factor, plus $1,000 for each additional financial service, plus endorsement fees, plus an expenditure component of $1,000 for the first $1,000,000 of expenditure and $1 for each additional $1,000. For a firm to which PIN applies, expenditure is the amount in its IN100 or IN30 annual regulatory return. Until the first annual return is submitted, the guidance to Rule 3.2.2 sets expenditure at zero. An insurer that is part of a Financial Stability Board global systemically important group, and a firm for which the DFSA is consolidated or lead supervisor, each add 100 percent of the table fee, and those two loadings are cumulative. The initial annual fee is the section 2.1 application fee, disregarding the Rule 2.1.1(3) supplement, multiplied by the number of whole calendar months from the licence grant to the end of the year and divided by 12. It is due within 21 days of the grant. Later annual fees are due on or before 1 January.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the Fees Module. UAE corporate tax under Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022 is 9 percent on taxable income that is not Qualifying Income of a Qualifying Free Zone Person, and 0 percent on Qualifying Income. Reinsurance services are a Qualifying Activity. Insurance activities regulated under Federal Decree-Law No. 48 of 2023 are an Excluded Activity, without prejudice to reinsurance services and headquarter services to Related Parties.

annual_filing_requirements: PIN Rule 6.5.1 requires the annual regulatory return to be submitted to the DFSA within four months of the insurer's reporting date. PIN Rule 6.2 requires the return to comprise the statements in PIN App10, supplementary notes, and a statement by directors. PIN Rule 6.5.2 requires the return, other than the statement by directors, to be submitted through the DFSA electronic prudential reporting system. The statement by directors need not be submitted, but it must be signed and a copy maintained under PIN Rules 6.5.3 and 6.5.4. PIN Rule 6.3.4 says a Class 1 captive insurer, and a protected cell company whose every cell is a Class 1 captive cell or a Class 2 captive cell, does not prepare a quarterly regulatory return unless the DFSA requires one in writing. The rules reviewed do not state an in-DIFC board-meeting requirement or a periodic on-site examination interval. The DFSA insurance summary says Federal Law No. 8 of 2004 requires DIFC insurers to conduct reinsurance only for risks situated in the UAE, and that direct insurance may be provided for risks situated in the DIFC and for risks situated offshore of the UAE. The contact page gives the office as Level 13, West Wing, The Gate, DIFC, postal address PO Box 75850, Dubai, UAE, and telephone +971 (0)4 362 1500, and it directs enquiries to an online form rather than displaying an email address.

name: Federated States of Micronesia
summary: The Federated States of Micronesia Insurance Board and the Insurance Commissioner license captive insurance companies under Chapter 10 of Title 37 of the FSM Code, the captive provisions added to the Insurance Act of 2006. Public Law No. 18-20, approved on 22 October 2013, sets four classes. A class 1 company insures its parent and affiliated companies or associations. A class 2 company may also insure related third-party businesses. A class 3 company is a member of a multiple corporate captive group. A class 4 company may also reinsure unaffiliated business. Section 1001(11), as amended by Public Law No. 18-20, describes that business as a company outside the parent's corporate system that has a business relationship with the parent or an affiliate, with commercial risks outside the Federated States of Micronesia, and says the definition does not include homeowners, personal automobile, or personal lines of FSM citizens. The same paragraph says the commercial risk is only reinsured by a class 4 company and is a maximum of 30 percent of net written premium after deducting ceded premium. Public Law No. 21-49, approved on 19 October 2019, requires minimum capital and surplus of $100,000 to be licensed. A multiple-corporate-captive core maintains $1,000,000 and each non-core member $100,000. A class 4 company maintains $5,000,000. The Commissioner may require more. The regulations published by the Insurance Board also set a class 2 test at the greater of $100,000, 20 percent of net premium income, or an amount the Commissioner determines, and a solvency margin at the greater of 20 percent of net premium income and 5 percent of loss reserves. Public Law No. 21-65, approved on 23 December 2019, places licensing with the Commissioner. Its purpose section says an application is deemed approved if it is neither approved nor denied within 30 days of receipt. The enacted section 1003A says the application is deemed approved if it is neither approved nor denied with 30 days of receipt. The nonrefundable application fee is $500 and the annual licence fee is $500. Section 1015 imposes a premium tax of 0.05 percent, due by 1 June, with an annual maximum of $20,000. Title 54, Chapter 3, as published by the Department of Finance and Administration, taxes a licensed captive as a major corporation at 21 percent of taxable income. The Insurance Board's 2025 annual report counts 23 licensed and active captives, out of 31 licensed since 2009, and says captives received $256 million of premium in 2025. The same report says two new captives were formed and licensed, says the Board approved one captive in 2025, and lists one licence dated 17 June 2025, so a single new-licence figure is not stored. The office is three board members, the Insurance Commissioner, and five employees. The report publishes info@fsminsuranceboard.com.
legislation: Title 37 of the Code of the Federated States of Micronesia, Chapter 10, Captive Insurance Act of 2006, as amended, and Title 54, Chapter 3, Corporate Income Tax Act of 2004, as amended
applicable_legislation: Chapter 10 was added to the Insurance Act of 2006. The 2014 code text published by the FSM Legal Information System states the classes, the six-month report, the premium tax, and the examination cycle as then in force. Public Law No. 18-20, approved on 22 October 2013, added the class 4 definition and the unaffiliated-business limit. Public Law No. 21-49, approved on 19 October 2019, replaced section 1007 and removed the separate $1,000,000 initial paid-in capital figure that the 2014 code still shows. Public Law No. 21-65, approved on 23 December 2019, amended section 1003, added the 30-day deeming rules in sections 1003A, 1008A, 1013A, and 1016A, and restated dividends and investments. Public Law No. 21-199, approved on 5 November 2020, added dormancy, and Public Law No. 22-02, approved on 27 May 2021, renumbered that section as section 1021. Captive regulations are published by the Insurance Board in its captive laws and regulations compilation. Corporate income tax is Title 54, Chapter 3, including section 321, in the compilation published by the Department of Finance and Administration. Public Law No. 16-19, approved on 27 December 2009, made captive insurance companies subject to that chapter regardless of capitalization.

min_capital.Class 1 and class 2: Section 1007, as amended by Public Law No. 21-49, requires a captive insurance company to maintain minimum capital and surplus of $100,000 before a licence is issued. The 2014 code's additional requirement of $1,000,000 initial paid-in capital was removed by that public law. Regulation IX in the Insurance Board compilation sets class 1 capital at $100,000 and class 2 capital at the greater of $100,000, 20 percent of net premium income, or an amount determined by the Commissioner.
min_capital.Class 3 multiple corporate captive: The core member maintains minimum capital and surplus of $1,000,000. Each non-core member maintains $100,000. Section 1001 also requires the core to hold at least 5 percent of each other member and requires each member to seat at least one core director. The core is licensed before the other members. Regulation IX states the same dollar floors and allows the Commissioner to set a higher core amount.
min_capital.Class 4: Minimum required capital and surplus of $5,000,000 under section 1007(3), as amended by Public Law No. 21-49. Regulation IX states the greater of $5,000,000 or an amount determined by the Commissioner. Section 1002(4), as amended by Public Law No. 18-20, says a class 4 company insures the risks of its parent and affiliated companies and/or associations and/or related third-party business and/or unaffiliated business and/or multiple corporate captive business. Section 1001(11) says unaffiliated commercial risk is only reinsured by a class 4 company, is outside the Federated States of Micronesia, does not include homeowners, personal automobile, or personal lines of FSM citizens, and is a maximum of 30 percent of net written premium after deducting ceded premium.
min_capital.Commissioner increase and form: The Commissioner may increase the minimum after taking into account the type, volume, and nature of the business and the potential risk retained. Capital and surplus may be any combination of cash, a letter of credit, investments permitted by section 1013, or any other security the Commissioner deems appropriate. A loan of the minimum capital and surplus required by section 1007 is prohibited.
min_capital.Solvency margin: Regulation X sets the minimum solvency margin at the greater of 20 percent of net premium income and 5 percent of the value of loss reserves. If net premium income is greater than $100 million, the captive may request that the Commissioner determine the margin. The 2014 code text does not restate this margin.
min_capital.Dormant captive: Section 1021, as renumbered by Public Law No. 22-02, allows a captive to apply for dormant status. The Commissioner may waive sections 1007, 1008, and 1013 if the captive certifies that it has no outstanding insurance liabilities on expired or terminated policies. The section does not state a substitute dollar floor.

tax_notes: Section 1015 requires each captive, on or before 1 June, to pay into the General Fund a tax of 0.05 percent of gross premiums for insurance on risks or property in the Federated States of Micronesia, and on risks and property elsewhere on which no premium tax is otherwise paid, for the year ending the preceding 31 March, less return premiums and less any reinsurance accepted. The annual maximum aggregate premium tax is $20,000. Two or more captives under common ownership and control are taxed as one. Common ownership and control is direct or indirect ownership of 80 percent or more of the voting stock, or of the surplus and voting power of mutual corporations. Multiyear premiums are prorated. Ten percent of the premium-tax revenue, or $150,000, whichever is greater, is transferred annually to the Insurance Board. Title 54, section 321, as published by the Department of Finance and Administration, imposes tax at 21 percent on the taxable income of every major corporation for a taxable year ending on or after 31 March 2011. A captive insurance company licensed under Title 37 is a major corporation regardless of capitalization. Taxable income is income before income taxes, determined under IFRS or GAAP as regularly used to calculate taxable income in the principal shareholder's place of incorporation or, if the shareholder is an individual, country of primary residence. A major corporation that is not engaging in business in the Federated States of Micronesia and that remits the section 321 tax is exempt from the gross-revenue tax for that taxable year. Foreign income tax is a non-refundable credit, capped at the FSM tax, with a carryforward of not more than seven years. The Insurance Board's captive-law page states the same 21 percent rate as a tax on net income and points to section 321 and to the section 1015 premium tax. The 2025 annual report says 2024 captive taxes were $17,126,164 and describes taxable income as underwriting revenue, interest on loans, and realized investment gains. That aggregate is not the section 1015 premium-tax cap.
contact_name: FSM Insurance Board
types_allowed: Class 1 captive insurance companies, insuring the parent and affiliated companies or associations
Class 2 captive insurance companies, which may also insure related third-party business
Class 3 multiple corporate captive insurance companies, with a core member and member captives
Class 4 captive insurance companies, which may reinsure unaffiliated business up to 30 percent of net written premium after ceded premium
Foreign captive insurance companies, defined as captives organized under the law of another jurisdiction
Dormant captive insurance companies holding dormant status under section 1021
regulator_staff_count: Three board members, the Insurance Commissioner, and five employees

fees.licensing_incorporation: Section 1003, as amended by Public Law No. 21-65, charges a nonrefundable fee of $500 for examining, investigating, and processing the licence application. The Commissioner may retain legal, financial, and examination services and charge the reasonable cost to the applicant. A captive that receives a licence pays a further licence fee of $500 for the year of registration, due within 30 days after registration or licensure. Fees are deposited into the revolving fund. National registrar incorporation fees are not set in section 1003.
fees.annual_fees: A yearly fee of $500 is due on or before the registration or licensure day and month each year. The 2025 annual report says the revolving fund receives application fees, licence fees, annual fees, and premium-tax amounts, and that charges for outside legal, financial, and examination services are also deposited there. At each fiscal year-end the fund is capped at $50,000 and the excess is transferred to the General Fund. Examination expenses are paid by the captive within 30 days of the warrant.
fees.premium_tax_rate: 0.05 percent of the gross premiums described in section 1015, due 1 June, with an annual maximum of $20,000. Captives under 80 percent common ownership are taxed as one captive. Separately, Title 54, section 321, taxes taxable income of a licensed captive at 21 percent. A major corporation that remits that tax and is not engaging in business in the Federated States of Micronesia is exempt from the gross-revenue tax for that year.

annual_filing_requirements: Section 1010 of the 2014 code requires, within six months of the fiscal year-end, a report of financial condition verified by the oath of two executive officers, audited financial statements prepared under generally accepted accounting principles or international accounting standards unless the Commissioner approves a modification, and an opinion of a loss-reserve specialist. The auditor and the loss-reserve specialist must be approved. For a multiple corporate captive, the core files for itself and the members do not file separately. Regulation VI in the Insurance Board compilation requires the audited annual report within 90 calendar days after the fiscal year-end. The Code states six months and the published regulation states 90 days. Both are recorded. Title 54, section 351, requires the major-corporation income-tax return, with the financial statements, by the last day of the sixth month after the taxable year. Section 352 requires the tax return by the last business day of that sixth month and a deposit of 50 percent of the prior year's tax by the end of the eighth month of the current fiscal year. A newly formed captive has no prior year and is not required to pay that deposit. Premium tax is due on or before 1 June. Section 1003 requires a principal place of business in the Federated States of Micronesia, a principal representative approved by the Commissioner, and an annual board meeting in the Federated States of Micronesia. Only the principal representative must be physically present for the quorum. The other directors may attend by telephone. English insurance and accounting records are kept at the principal office for examination. Section 1011 requires an examination at least once in three years, which the Commissioner may extend to five years on petition, and whenever the Commissioner determines it to be prudent. The 2025 annual report says no captive examinations were conducted in fiscal year 2025. A dormant captive's section 1010 reports apply only to the first reports due after it becomes dormant, and the Commissioner may defer the examination, while the dormant captive continues. A captive may not insure the risks of individual citizens of the Federated States of Micronesia. Dividends out of capital or surplus require the Commissioner's prior approval, and a dividend proposal that is neither approved nor denied within 30 days of receipt is deemed approved.

captive_administrator.name: FSM Insurance Board

licensing_speed: The purpose section of Public Law No. 21-65 says an application is deemed approved if it is neither approved nor denied within 30 days of receipt. The enacted section 1003A says the application shall be deemed approved if it is neither approved nor denied with 30 days of receipt by the Insurance Commissioner. Sections 1008A, 1013A, and 1016A use "within 30 days" for a dividend, a loan or investment, and a business-plan change.

name: Florida
summary: Florida licenses captive insurers under Part V of Chapter 628, Florida Statutes. The part originated in chapter 82-243, Laws of Florida (1982). Chapter 2012-151 specified formation, capital, reporting, and reinsurance in more detail, and chapter 2026-72, approved on 11 May 2026 and effective 1 July 2026, added protected cell captive insurance companies. The Office of Insurance Regulation licenses pure, industrial insured, special purpose, and protected cell captives, and separately licenses captive reinsurance companies. A pure captive insures its parent, affiliated companies, and controlled unaffiliated businesses. An industrial insured captive insures the industrial insureds that own it, and their affiliates, and may reinsure insurers only on those risks. A special purpose captive does not meet another captive definition and may insure only its parent. A protected cell captive insures participants through participant contracts and segregates each cell from the others and from the general account. A captive reinsurance company is a stock corporation, wholly owned by a qualifying reinsurer parent, and may not insure risks directly. Unimpaired paid-in capital is at least $100,000 for a pure or protected cell stock captive and $200,000 for an industrial insured stock captive. A nonprofit pure captive maintains unrestricted net assets of at least $250,000, and a nonprofit protected cell captive maintains at least $100,000. Unimpaired surplus is at least $150,000 for a pure captive, $100,000 for a protected cell captive, $300,000 for an industrial insured stock captive, and $500,000 for an industrial insured mutual captive. Special purpose amounts are set by the Office. A captive reinsurer maintains capital or surplus of at least the greater of $300 million or 10 percent of reserves. Section 624.509 taxes direct premiums on Florida risks at 1.75 percent and omits premiums on reinsurance accepted. A salary credit and a credit for Florida corporate income tax paid are together limited to 65 percent of the premium tax after the deductions named in the Department of Revenue instructions. The Office's 2026 captive application states that $1,525 is payable when the application is filed, under sections 624.501(17) and 628.905(4), together with the $1,000 annual license tax under section 624.501(3). The Office does not publish a captive census or a captive-unit headcount. Its captive overview page still describes three captive-insurance types and does not describe the protected cell captives added on 1 July 2026.
legislation: Chapter 628, Part V, Florida Statutes, sections 628.901 to 628.921, as amended by chapter 2026-72, Laws of Florida
applicable_legislation: Part V originated in chapter 82-243, Laws of Florida. Chapter 2012-151 (House Bill 1101) amended the formation, capital, reporting, and reinsurance provisions. Chapter 2013-209 also amended the part. Chapter 2026-72, Committee Substitute for Committee Substitute for House Bill 883, was approved by the Governor on 11 May 2026, filed with the Secretary of State the same day, and took effect on 1 July 2026. It added protected cell definitions and section 628.921. Capital and net assets are section 628.907. Surplus is section 628.908. Captive reinsurance capital is section 628.914. Licensing and the captive fee are section 628.905. Reports are section 628.911. Which other Insurance Code provisions apply is section 628.909. Incorporation is section 628.910. The general fee schedule is section 624.501. Premium tax is section 624.509, and Florida Administrative Code Rule 12B-8.001 lists captives in the 1.75 percent computation. The Department of Revenue's 2026 Form DR-908 instructions state the 65 percent combined credit limit under sections 624.509(4) and 624.509(5).

min_capital.Pure captive, stock: At least $100,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital (section 628.907(1)(b)) and at least $150,000 of unimpaired surplus (section 628.908(1)(a)).
min_capital.Pure captive, nonprofit: At least $250,000 of unrestricted net assets (section 628.907(2)(b)). Section 628.908(1)(a) also requires at least $150,000 of unimpaired surplus for a pure captive and does not exclude a nonprofit pure captive. Contributions to a nonprofit captive must be cash, a cash equivalent, or an irrevocable letter of credit issued by a Florida-chartered bank or a Federal Reserve member bank with a Florida branch, or as approved by the Office (section 628.907(3)).
min_capital.Industrial insured captive, stock: At least $200,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital (section 628.907(1)(c)) and at least $300,000 of unimpaired surplus (section 628.908(1)(c)).
min_capital.Industrial insured captive, mutual: At least $500,000 of unimpaired surplus (section 628.908(1)(d)). Section 628.907 does not set a separate paid-in capital amount for a mutual industrial insured captive. It may be incorporated as a mutual insurer without capital stock (section 628.910(2)(b)).
min_capital.Protected cell captive: At least $100,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital if incorporated with capital stock, or at least $100,000 of unrestricted net assets if incorporated as a nonprofit (section 628.907(1)(a) and (2)(a)), and at least $100,000 of unimpaired surplus (section 628.908(1)(b)). Section 628.921, effective 1 July 2026, does not set a separate dollar floor for an individual protected cell. When a cell is established, assets attributed to it must at least equal the reserves and other insurance liabilities attributed to that cell. The company's capital and surplus must at all times be available to pay expenses of or claims against the company.
min_capital.Special purpose captive: The Office sets the unimpaired paid-in capital, the unrestricted net assets of a nonprofit, and the unimpaired surplus after considering the business plan, feasibility study, pro forma financial statements and projections, and the risks to be insured (sections 628.907(1)(d), 628.907(2)(c), and 628.908(1)(e)).
min_capital.Captive reinsurance company: Capital or unimpaired surplus of at least the greater of $300 million or 10 percent of reserves. The test is capital or surplus, not both. Surplus may be cash or securities permitted by Part II of Chapter 625. The Office may prescribe additional capital or surplus (section 628.914).
min_capital.Additional capital and conditional licen: The Office may prescribe additional capital or net assets based on the type, volume, and nature of the business. Those additional amounts must be cash, a cash equivalent, an irrevocable letter of credit from a Florida-chartered bank or a Federal Reserve member bank with a Florida branch, or as approved by the Office, or securities invested under Part II of Chapter 625 (section 628.907(5)). The Office may issue a license conditioned on evidence of the minimum capital or surplus. Until that evidence is provided, the captive may not issue a policy, assume a liability, or otherwise provide coverage. The Office may revoke the conditional license if the evidence is not provided within the period it sets, which may not exceed one year (sections 628.907(4) and 628.908(2)).

tax_notes: Section 628.909 applies Chapter 624 to captive insurance companies and to industrial insured captives, except listed sections that do not include section 624.509. Section 624.509(1) requires each insurer, on or before 1 March, to pay the Department of Revenue a tax on premiums, assessments, membership fees, policy fees, and gross deposits received during the preceding calendar year. The rate in section 624.509(1)(a) is 1.75 percent of the gross amount of receipts on life and health policies covering Florida residents and on other policies and contracts covering property, subjects, or risks located, resident, or to be performed in Florida. Annuity receipts are taxed at 1 percent under paragraph (b), and direct written bail-bond premiums are taxed at 1.75 percent under paragraph (c). The paragraph (a) base omits premiums on reinsurance accepted and subtracts return premiums or assessments. It does not allow a deduction for reinsurance ceded, cash surrender values, prompt-payment discounts or refunds, or dividends credited to policyholders. Rule 12B-8.001 expressly applies that 1.75 percent rate to insurance issued by a captive or industrial captive insurer under Part V of Chapter 628. Section 624.509(5) allows a credit equal to 15 percent of salaries paid to employees located or based in Florida and covered by Chapter 443. An affiliated group that includes at least one insurer writing Florida premiums may instead use the alternative salary credit, if it elected that method on or before 1 August 2005. Section 624.509(4) credits Florida corporate income tax paid against the premium tax. The Department of Revenue's 2026 Form DR-908 instructions state that the corporate-income-tax credit and the salary credit together may not exceed 65 percent of the premium tax due after deductions for the excise taxes paid to the Firefighters' and Municipal Police Officers' Retirement Trust Funds and for the workers' compensation assessment. Part V does not state a captive-specific corporate income-tax rate or an in-lieu exemption from it. The Florida corporate income-tax rate was not taken from Chapter 220 in this review. A protected cell's premium tax follows the cell on a conversion or disaffiliation: the prior entity is responsible for premium tax on transactions before the final date, and the successor is responsible on and after that date (section 628.921(9)(e), chapter 2026-72).
contact_name: Property and Casualty Company Admissions, Florida Office of Insurance Regulation
types_allowed: Pure captive insurance companies, insuring the parent, affiliated companies, controlled unaffiliated businesses, or a combination of them

Industrial insured captive insurance companies. An industrial insured has gross assets above $50 million, at least 100 full-time employees, buys through a full-time insurance manager or buyer or a licensed property and casualty agent, broker, or consultant, and pays at least $200,000 of annual premium for each line, or at least $75,000 for a line in excess of at least $25 million in the annual aggregate
Special purpose captive insurance companies, which do not meet another captive definition and may insure only the parent
Protected cell captive insurance companies, effective 1 July 2026, insuring participants through participant contracts, with incorporated and unincorporated protected cells

Captive reinsurance companies, wholly owned by a qualifying reinsurer parent that holds a certificate of authority or qualifies for credit for reinsurance under section 624.610(3), has consolidated GAAP net worth of at least $500 million, and has a consolidated debt to total capital ratio no greater than 0.50

Pure captives incorporated as stock insurers or as public-benefit, mutual-benefit, or religious nonprofit corporations; industrial insured captives incorporated as stock or mutual insurers; protected cell captives incorporated as stock insurers, mutual corporations, nonprofit corporations, or limited liability companies

fees.licensing_incorporation: Section 628.905(4) requires a nonrefundable fee of $1,500 to process the license application of a captive insurance company or a captive reinsurance company. Section 624.501(17) charges $25 to file an application for a permit to form an insurer under Chapter 628. The Office's captive application package, in the 2026 company-admissions forms, states that the applicant pays $1,525 under those two sections when the application is filed. The same package also requires the $1,000 annual license tax under section 624.501(3) at filing. Both amounts are nonrefundable. Section 628.905(4)(b) allows a $5 fee for a document that needs a certification of authenticity or an Office signature. Fingerprint processing is charged at cost under section 624.501(23). The amount is not fixed in that subsection. Organization fees payable to the Department of State are those required by the Florida Business Corporation Act or the Florida Nonprofit Corporation Act. Part V does not set the dollar amount. The captive overview page states an initial license application fee of $1,500 and does not mention the $25 permit fee.
fees.annual_fees: Section 628.905(4)(a) requires an annual renewal fee of $1,000. Section 624.501(3) imposes an annual license tax of $1,000 on each domestic, foreign, and alien insurer, and Chapter 624 applies to these captives. The Office's 2026 application describes the $1,000 due at filing as the section 624.501(3) annual license tax. The captive overview page describes a $1,000 annual renewal fee. The pages reviewed do not say whether those two statutory $1,000 amounts are collected once or twice. A license authorizes business until the next 1 March and may then be renewed (section 628.905(5)). Section 624.501(4) sets a $250 fee for an insurer's annual statement and $250 for a quarterly statement. Section 628.911(1) says a captive may not be required to make any annual report except as Part V provides, so those statement fees are not restated here as captive fees.
fees.premium_tax_rate: 1.75 percent of the section 624.509(1)(a) gross receipts on Florida risks, due 1 March. Premiums on reinsurance accepted are omitted. Return premiums are deducted. Reinsurance ceded, surrender values, prompt-payment discounts, and policyholder dividends are not deducted. Annuities are taxed at 1 percent. The 15 percent Florida-salary credit and the credit for Florida corporate income tax paid together may not exceed 65 percent of the premium tax after the firefighter, municipal police, and workers' compensation assessment deductions stated in the 2026 Form DR-908 instructions.

annual_filing_requirements: Section 628.911(1) says a captive insurance company may not be required to make any annual report except as Part V provides. On or before 1 March, a captive insurance company or a captive reinsurance company submits a report of its financial condition, verified by the oath of two executive officers. The report uses generally accepted accounting principles unless the Office approves statutory accounting principles, with the modifications the Office requires or accepts, plus any additional information the Office requires. The Financial Services Commission may adopt the report form by rule. A captive may apply to report on a fiscal year-end consistent with its parent's fiscal year. If that date is granted, the report is due 60 days after the fiscal year-end. A protected cell captive must file the financial reports the Office requires, and each report must include accounting statements for the financial experience of each protected cell. It must notify the Office in writing within 10 business days of any protected cell that is insolvent or unable to meet its claims or expenses. The Office's captive page states that a captive reinsurance company must file an annual actuarial opinion on loss and loss-adjustment-expense reserves from an independent actuary who is not an employee of the company or its affiliates, and that loss reserves may be discounted at treasury rates under section 628.912. A captive must hold at least one board meeting each year in Florida, keep its principal place of business in Florida, and appoint a resident registered agent (section 628.905(2)). A captive incorporated in Florida as a corporation or nonprofit must have at least one Florida-resident director (section 628.910(7)). It may not have fewer than three incorporators, of whom at least two are Florida residents (section 628.910(3)). Chapter 624 applies except the sections excluded by section 628.909, so the Office's Chapter 624 examination authority applies. Part V does not state a separate examination interval.

captive_administrator.name: Property and Casualty Company Admissions, Florida Office of Insurance Regulation

licensing_speed: Section 628.905 does not set a number of days for a decision. If the Office is satisfied that the filing complies, it may grant a license until the next 1 March, when the license may be renewed. The Company Admissions page states that, after an application is accepted and considered complete, the Office strives to conclude the review within 60 days. Sections 628.907(4) and 628.908(2) separately allow a conditional license, for no more than one year, while the captive produces evidence of the minimum capital or surplus. The captive may not provide coverage during that period.
