name: France
summary: France has no separate captive insurance statute. Article L.350-2 of the Code des assurances, created by Ordinance No. 2015-378 of 2 April 2015 and in force since 1 January 2016, defines an entreprise captive d'assurance and an entreprise captive de réassurance. Both are authorized and supervised by the Autorité de contrôle prudentiel et de résolution as insurance or reinsurance undertakings under the Code des assurances and Solvency II. A captive insurer's object is exclusively the insurance of risks of the undertaking or undertakings to which it belongs, or of other undertakings in its group. A captive reinsurer's object is the same cover in reinsurance, and its head office is in France. The absolute floor of the minimum capital requirement, set by Article A.352-29 since 29 October 2022, is EUR 2,700,000 for non-life insurance, including a captive insurer, EUR 4,000,000 where classes 10 to 15 are covered and for life insurance, EUR 3,900,000 for a reinsurer, and EUR 1,300,000 for a captive reinsurer. The minimum capital requirement must also lie between 25 and 45 percent of the solvency capital requirement. Article 6 of the Finance Law for 2023, codified as Article 39 quinquies G, II, of the General Tax Code, lets an eligible captive reinsurer deduct a provision pour résilience. The annual allocation is limited to 90 percent of the relevant technical result, and the stock of the provision may not exceed ten times the average minimum capital requirement over three years. The ordinary corporate income-tax rate is 25 percent. The ACPR's captive-reinsurance guide, published on 12 November 2024, said that 17 captive reinsurers had already been authorized. That is the latest official count found. It is not a later census of licences in force, and it does not count captive insurers. The guide tells applicants to write to the Authorizations Directorate at 2785-secretariat-direction-ut@acpr.banque-france.fr. Once a file is complete, silence for six months is an implicit refusal under Articles R.321-4 and R.321-5-3.
legislation: Code des assurances, including Articles L.350-2, L.321-1, L.321-1-1, R.321-4, R.321-5-3, R.352-29, and A.352-29, and Article 39 quinquies G of the Code général des impôts
applicable_legislation: Article L.350-2 was created by Ordinance No. 2015-378 of 2 April 2015 and has been in force since 1 January 2016. It defines entreprise captive d'assurance and entreprise captive de réassurance. Authorization of insurance undertakings is Article L.321-1, and authorization of reinsurance undertakings is Article L.321-1-1. The six-month implicit refusal is Article R.321-4 for insurance and Article R.321-5-3 for reinsurance. The minimum capital requirement is Article R.352-29, as amended by Decree No. 2022-1018 of 20 July 2022, in force on 1 October 2022. The euro floors are Article A.352-29, created by the order of 21 October 2022 and in force on 29 October 2022. The ACPR states the same floors in its authorization guidance, citing Articles R.352-29 and A.352-29. The provision pour résilience is Article 39 quinquies G, II, of the Code général des impôts, introduced by Article 6 of Law No. 2022-1726 of 30 December 2022 (Finance Law for 2023) and amended by Article 4 of Law No. 2023-1322 of 29 December 2023. The 90 percent and ten-times-MCR limits are Article 16 A, II, of Annex II to the General Tax Code. Accounting recognition is Article R.343-8, 12° bis, of the Code des assurances. Corporate income tax is Article 219 of the General Tax Code, whose normal rate is 25 percent. The ACPR contribution for supervision costs is described, by reference to Article L.612-20 of the Monetary and Financial Code, in the ACPR captive-reinsurance guide of 12 November 2024.

min_capital.Captive reinsurance undertaking: Absolute floor of EUR 1,300,000 (Article A.352-29, point iii). The ACPR authorization note states the same EUR 1,300,000 floor for a captive reinsurer and EUR 3,900,000 for other reinsurers.
min_capital.How the minimum is set: Article R.352-29 sets the minimum capital requirement as an amount of eligible basic own funds below which policyholders and cedants would face an unacceptable risk if the undertaking continued. The linear function is calibrated to an 85 percent value-at-risk of basic own funds over one year. Without displacing the absolute floor, the minimum capital requirement must lie between 25 and 45 percent of the solvency capital requirement, including any capital add-on under Article L.352-3. It is calculated at least quarterly and reported to the ACPR. The euro floors are fixed by order under Article A.352-29.
min_capital.Non-life insurance, including a captive: Absolute floor of EUR 2,700,000 (Article A.352-29, point i). If any of the risks in classes 10 to 15 of Article R.321-1 is covered, the floor may not be lower than the life floor in point ii.
min_capital.Life insurance, including a captive insu: Absolute floor of EUR 4,000,000 (Article A.352-29, point ii).
min_capital.Composite insurance: The floor is the sum of the non-life and life floors (Article R.352-29, I, d, iv).
min_capital.Reinsurance undertaking: Absolute floor of EUR 3,900,000 (Article A.352-29, point iii).

tax_notes: Captive insurers and reinsurers are subject to corporate income tax. Article 219, I, of the General Tax Code, in force as amended on 21 February 2026, sets the normal rate at 25 percent. Article 219, I, b, sets a 15 percent rate, for financial years opened from 1 January 2002, on taxable profit up to EUR 42,500 in a twelve-month period, where turnover does not exceed EUR 10 million. That reduced rate also requires the company's capital to be fully paid up and held continuously, at least 75 percent, by natural persons or by a company that itself meets those conditions. A captive owned by a corporate group will commonly fail that holding test. The captive-specific relief is the provision pour résilience in Article 39 quinquies G, II. It is available to a captive reinsurer under Article L.350-2, 3°, that is owned by an undertaking other than a financial undertaking within Article L.310-3, 12°, and whose object is exclusively the reinsurance of risks of undertakings that are not financial undertakings. The provision covers accepted reinsurance of the categories listed in Article A.344-2 as in force on 31 December 2022: professional and agricultural property damage, natural catastrophes, general liability, pecuniary loss, damage and pecuniary loss from attacks on information and communication systems, and transport. Article 16 A, II, of Annex II limits the annual allocation to 90 percent of the sum of the technical profits of those categories, and limits the total provision to ten times the average minimum capital requirement over the last three years. Unused annual allocations are brought back into taxable profit in the sixteenth year. Risks reserved under paragraph II cannot also be reserved under paragraph I. The provision is recognized under Article R.343-8, 12° bis. The decree of 7 June 2024 applies the Annex II limits to financial years opened from 1 January 2024. No separate insurance-premium-tax rate for a captive was extracted from these articles. The ACPR guide states that supervised undertakings pay an annual contribution for supervision costs. It says Article L.612-20, II, B, of the Monetary and Financial Code bases that contribution on premiums issued and accepted in the last closed year, and that Article L.612-20, III, 2°, sets a rate between 0.15 and 0.25 per thousand and a minimum between EUR 500 and EUR 1,500. The rate fixed for a particular year inside that band was not extracted.
contact_name: Direction des autorisations, Secrétariat général de l'ACPR
types_allowed: Captive insurance undertakings (entreprises captives d'assurance) as defined in Article L.350-2, 1°, authorized as insurance undertakings

Captive reinsurance undertakings (entreprises captives de réassurance) as defined in Article L.350-2, 3°, authorized as reinsurance undertakings. The ACPR guide says a captive reinsurer is formed as a société anonyme, a société d'assurance mutuelle, or a société européenne
New French captive reinsurers and captive reinsurers transferring their head office to France from the European Economic Area
No protected-cell or incorporated-cell regime is stated in the Code des assurances articles reviewed

fees.licensing_incorporation: No fixed captive application fee is stated in the Code des assurances articles or the ACPR guide reviewed. The guide says a project is first presented to the Authorizations Directorate and the complete file is then filed through the ACPR portal.
fees.annual_fees: The ACPR guide says every supervised undertaking pays an annual contribution for supervision costs. It describes the base as premiums issued and accepted in the last closed financial year, under Article L.612-20, II, B, of the Monetary and Financial Code, and a rate between 0.15 and 0.25 per thousand, with a minimum between EUR 500 and EUR 1,500, under Article L.612-20, III, 2°. The order setting the rate for a given year inside that band was not extracted.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No captive premium-tax rate was extracted from the articles reviewed. Corporate income tax is 25 percent under Article 219, I. The 15 percent rate on the first EUR 42,500 applies only where turnover does not exceed EUR 10 million and the fully paid-up capital is held at least 75 percent by natural persons, or by a company meeting the same test. Eligible captive reinsurers may deduct the provision pour résilience, capped each year at 90 percent of the relevant technical result and in total at ten times the three-year average minimum capital requirement.

annual_filing_requirements: After authorization, the ACPR guide says a captive reinsurer is subject to the Solvency II reporting obligations, filed from the first year through the OneGate portal. Article R.352-29, IV, requires the minimum capital requirement to be calculated at least quarterly and transmitted to the ACPR. The guide says a change of direct or indirect ownership that crosses a threshold upward, and keeping a financial year-end other than 31 December beyond the first year unless the authorization already allowed it, need prior ACPR approval. Changes of bylaws, appointment or renewal of an effective manager or a key-function holder, a downward ownership-threshold crossing, and a change of provider of critical or important activities must be notified, and the ACPR may object. The guide requires at least two effective managers, so that the four-eyes principle is met, and an identified holder of each of the four key functions: actuarial, risk management, compliance, and internal audit. Proportionality may allow one person to combine roles, except that internal audit is not combined except in the cases the ACPR notice describes, and one person may not hold more than three functions. The ACPR may withdraw the authorization if the conditions for it are no longer met, and it may record that the authorization has lapsed if it is unused. A standard number of days for the annual quantitative templates, beyond the quarterly minimum-capital transmission, was not extracted from the national reporting page linked in the guide.

captive_administrator.name: Direction des autorisations, Secrétariat général de l'Autorité de contrôle prudentiel et de résolution

licensing_speed: The ACPR captive-reinsurance guide states that, once the file is complete, the ACPR has a regulatory period of six months to decide. Completeness is the transmission, in usable form, of every document required by the annexes to Instruction 2015-I-15. Article R.321-4, for an insurance undertaking, and Article R.321-5-3, for a reinsurance undertaking, provide that the absence of a notification at the end of six months from receipt of a duly completed application is an implicit refusal. The six months are extended if the ACPR defers the decision under Article L.321-2. Authorization is not automatic. The guide says the decision is taken by the ACPR's Supervisory College.

name: Georgia
summary: Georgia licenses captive insurance companies under the Georgia Captive Insurance Company Act, Chapter 41 of Title 33, enacted in 1988 and administered by the Captives Division of the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire. The chapter covers pure, association, agency, industrial insured, and sponsored captives, and risk retention group captives. A sponsored captive may use incorporated or unincorporated protected cells. House Bill 348, effective 1 June 2025, amended the permissible-business section so that a captive may engage in any insurance or reinsurance the Commissioner deems reasonable, still subject to the ownership and risk limits in O.C.G.A. section 33-41-3. Workers' compensation and motor-vehicle policies must meet Georgia's minimum coverage requirements. Surplus floors are $250,000 for a pure, agency, or sponsored captive and $500,000 for an association captive, an industrial insured captive, or a risk retention group. A dormant captive maintains at least $25,000. Direct premium tax is 0.4 percent on the first $20 million and 0.3 percent thereafter. Assumed-reinsurance premium tax runs from 0.225 percent down to 0.025 percent across $20 million bands. The annual maximum is $100,000. The statute does not state a minimum premium tax. The license fee is $600 at application and the renewal fee is $500 each later year. The Division's formation page says proposed articles are approved or disapproved within 45 days and the certificate of authority within 90 days, with a further 90-day extension available under O.C.G.A. section 33-3-15. The Captives Division contact page publishes captivedivision@oci.ga.gov and does not name a captive program head or a section headcount. The Division pages reviewed do not publish a current captive census.
legislation: Georgia Captive Insurance Company Act, O.C.G.A. Title 33, Chapter 41, and Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Chapter 120-2-45
applicable_legislation: O.C.G.A. Title 33, Chapter 41, Article 1, enacted by Ga. L. 1988, p. 966, and Article 2 on sponsored captive insurance companies, enacted in 2019. House Bill 348, Act 258, effective 1 June 2025, amended sections 33-41-2 and 33-41-3. Capital and surplus are section 33-41-8. Premium tax is section 33-41-22. Reports are section 33-41-15. Examinations are section 33-41-16. The certificate of dormancy is section 33-41-23. License and renewal fees are Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Rule 120-2-45-.12. Annual statements are Rule 120-2-45-.07. Audits are Rule 120-2-45-.09. Examinations and the organizational-examination fee are Rule 120-2-45-.08. Premium-tax filing is Rule 120-2-45-.13.

min_capital.Pure captive: At least $250,000 in surplus. The Commissioner sets the amount individually and may require more based on the business plan (O.C.G.A. section 33-41-8(a)(1)).
min_capital.Sponsored captive: At least $250,000 in surplus under section 33-41-8(a)(6), and at least $250,000 in capital and surplus under section 33-41-101(9)(B), available to pay expenses and claims of the sponsored captive. Article 2 does not state a separate dollar floor for an unincorporated protected cell.
min_capital.Dormant captive: At least $25,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus while a certificate of dormancy is in force. If the Commissioner allows dormancy while liabilities remain, the Commissioner may require more capital, surplus, and reserves (section 33-41-23).
min_capital.Form and deposit: Minimum capital or surplus of up to $500,000 is held in cash, FDIC-insured certificates of deposit, insured savings accounts or certificates, or letters of credit that meet section 33-41-9. Additional capital above $500,000 may be held in eligible investments under section 33-11-5, shareholder obligations secured by letters of credit, or other investments the Commissioner approves. An association captive, an industrial insured captive, and a risk retention group must deposit with the state before the certificate of authority is issued. The current text of section 33-41-8(c) requires that deposit and does not state its dollar amount.

tax_notes: O.C.G.A. section 33-41-22 imposes the captive tax in lieu of any other taxes imposed by Title 33. Direct premiums, after return premiums and policyholder dividends or premium deposits returned or credited, are taxed at 0.4 percent on the first $20 million and 0.3 percent on each dollar thereafter. A risk retention group captive is subject to that direct-premium tax only on coverages within Georgia. Assumed-reinsurance premium is taxed at 0.225 percent on the first $20 million, 0.150 percent on the next $20 million, 0.050 percent on the next $20 million, and 0.025 percent thereafter. Reinsurance tax does not apply to risks taxed on a direct basis, or to a qualifying assumption of loss reserves and other liabilities of another insurer under common ownership and control that the Commissioner verifies is part of a plan to discontinue that insurer. If the calculated tax exceeds $100,000 in a year, the tax is $100,000. The section does not state a minimum tax. Two or more captives under common ownership and control, other than sponsored captives, are taxed as one captive. Common ownership and control means more than 50 percent of the voting securities or membership interests. A protected cell is a captive for this tax. The aggregation rule applies to each cell and its participants, and the sponsored captive collects and remits the cells' tax. The annual return and payment are due 1 March under Rule 120-2-45-.13. A late return or payment draws a $5,000 penalty. An extension of not more than 30 days may be granted, with interest of 1 percent per month. Rule 120-2-45-.13(3) says a risk retention group files and pays premium tax under O.C.G.A. section 33-40-5. A separate section 33-40-5 rate is not restated here. A dormant captive that holds a certificate of dormancy is not liable for the section 33-41-22 tax. No Georgia corporate income-tax rate for captives is stated in Chapter 41.
contact_name: Captives Division, Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire
types_allowed: Agency captive insurance companies, reinsuring placed insurance or annuity contracts or service-contract liability
Incorporated protected cells and unincorporated protected cells
Risk retention group captive insurance companies
Dormant captive insurance companies holding a certificate of dormancy

fees.licensing_incorporation: Rule 120-2-45-.12 requires a $600 license fee when the application for a certificate of authority is filed. If the Commissioner requires an organizational examination, Rule 120-2-45-.08 requires $3,000 payable to the appointed examiner, and the Commissioner may require a higher amount in writing. O.C.G.A. section 33-41-10(c) also requires the applicant to pay the costs of examining, investigating, and processing the original or renewal application. Corporate formation fees payable to the Georgia Secretary of State are not set in Chapter 41.
fees.annual_fees: A renewal fee of $500 is due for each year after the initial year of licensure (Rule 120-2-45-.12). A certificate of dormancy is renewed every five years for $500 (O.C.G.A. section 33-41-23(b)(3)).
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums: 0.4 percent on the first $20 million and 0.3 percent thereafter. A risk retention group is taxed under section 33-41-22 only on direct premiums for Georgia coverages, and Rule 120-2-45-.13(3) points risk-retention-group premium-tax filing to O.C.G.A. section 33-40-5. Assumed reinsurance: 0.225 percent, 0.150 percent, 0.050 percent, and 0.025 percent on successive $20 million bands. No minimum is stated in section 33-41-22. Annual maximum $100,000. Due 1 March. Late filing or payment penalty $5,000.

annual_filing_requirements: Each captive files the reports of its business affairs required by O.C.G.A. section 33-3-21, as section 33-41-15 provides. Rule 120-2-45-.07 requires, on or before 1 March, a report of financial condition as of the preceding 31 December, verified by the oath of an executive officer. A pure captive elects generally accepted accounting principles or statutory accounting principles. An industrial insured captive and an association captive use statutory accounting principles. An industrial insured captive, an association captive, and a risk retention group file the NAIC property-and-casualty blank by 1 March. An industrial insured or association captive that directly writes workers' compensation, and every risk retention group, also files quarterly NAIC blanks as of 31 March, 30 June, and 30 September, due 15 May, 15 August, and 15 November. Rule 120-2-45-.09 requires an audited financial report by 30 June. The audit includes an opinion on the adequacy of loss and loss-expense reserves by a Fellow of the Casualty Actuarial Society, a member of the American Academy of Actuaries, or another person who has demonstrated competence in loss-reserve evaluation and whom the Commissioner approves. The premium-tax return is due 1 March. A sponsored captive's annual financial report includes the financial experience of each protected cell. The Commissioner may examine a captive at any time, and Rule 120-2-45-.08 says an examination occurs no less often than once every five years unless the Commissioner makes a written finding that a longer period is warranted. At least one director or manager is a Georgia resident, and the company reports a director or manager change within 30 days. A material change that is not disapproved within 30 days after submission is deemed approved. A dormant captive files a financial-condition report by 1 March and does not file the other annual forms, fees, or documents that Chapter 41 would otherwise require. Filings and payments are submitted through the GIMS portal.

captive_administrator.name: Captives Division, Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire

licensing_speed: The Division's formation page states that proposed articles of incorporation are approved or disapproved within 45 days, and that the certificate of authority is then approved or disapproved within 90 days. The Division may extend that certificate review by another 90 days under O.C.G.A. section 33-3-15 by written notice. A redomestication application is approved or disapproved within 45 days under Rule 120-2-45-.17. O.C.G.A. section 33-41-10(d) says that, once the Commissioner is satisfied the application complies, the certificate is issued promptly and authorizes business until 30 June.

regulator.name: Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire, Captives Division

name: Germany
summary: Germany has no separate captive insurance act. A captive is authorized as an insurer or a reinsurer under the Versicherungsaufsichtsgesetz of 1 April 2015, last amended by the Act of 25 September 2026, and is supervised by the Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht. Section 8 requires an undertaking with its seat in Germany to obtain permission before it carries on business. Permission may be granted to a stock corporation, including a European company, a mutual insurance association, or a public-law corporation or institution. The head office must be in Germany. A reinsurer is authorized only for reinsurance. Directive 2009/138/EC, Article 13, defines a firmeneigenes Versicherungsunternehmen and a firmeneigenes Rückversicherungsunternehmen as an insurer or reinsurer owned by a financial undertaking that is not itself an insurer or reinsurer, or by a non-financial undertaking, and writing only the risks of the owner or of the group. The VAG uses the same captive description in section 45(5), item 10. The absolute floor of the minimum capital requirement is set by section 1(2) of the Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung: EUR 2.7 million for health and property-casualty business that does not cover classes 10 to 15, including a captive insurer; EUR 4 million if any of those classes is covered; EUR 4 million for life, including a captive insurer; EUR 3.9 million for a reinsurer; and EUR 1.3 million for a captive reinsurer. BaFin's reinsurance-authorization notice of 1 March 2017 still prints the earlier floors of EUR 3.6 million and EUR 1.2 million, and it says only the law in force when the application is made is binding. The fee now in force for an initial permission under section 8(1) is EUR 32,259 under item 19.2 of the Finanzdienstleistungsaufsichtsgebührenverordnung. Corporate income tax is 15 percent through the 2027 assessment year. Insurance premium tax is generally 19 percent, and section 4(1) of the Versicherungsteuergesetz exempts a reinsurance premium. BaFin's 2025 annual report does not publish a captive count. It reported 3,084 employees at 31 December 2025. The organisation chart of 1 October 2026 places captive supervision in Referat VA 46 and does not give that unit's headcount.
legislation: Versicherungsaufsichtsgesetz of 1 April 2015, and the Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung, section 1
applicable_legislation: Versicherungsaufsichtsgesetz of 1 April 2015 (BGBl. I p. 434), last amended by Article 3 of the Act of 25 September 2026 (BGBl. 2026 I No. 275). Permission, legal form, and the head-office requirement are section 8. The application and the business plan are section 9. Refusal grounds are section 11. The scope of permission is section 10. The minimum capital requirement is section 122, and its calculation and quarterly report are section 123. The absolute floors are section 1(2) of the Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung. Own funds covering the solvency capital requirement and the minimum capital requirement are sections 89, 94, and 95. The solvency and financial condition report is section 40. Annual accounts are submitted under section 37. Relief from reporting that is more frequent than annual is section 45, which lists a captive writing only the risks of its industrial or commercial group as one proportionality factor. Withdrawal of permission is section 304. Directive 2009/138/EC, Article 13(2) and Article 13(5), defines the captive insurer and the captive reinsurer. Article 25 requires a judicial remedy if the supervisor has not decided an application within six months of receipt. The initial-permission fee is item 19.2 of the Finanzdienstleistungsaufsichtsgebührenverordnung of 2 September 2021, last amended by Article 4 of the Act of 25 September 2026. Corporate income tax is section 23 of the Körperschaftsteuergesetz. Insurance premium tax is the Versicherungsteuergesetz, sections 4 and 6. BaFin's reinsurance-authorization notice of 1 March 2017 describes the reinsurance application. It still states the pre-indexation floors and the former EUR 10,000 fee.

min_capital.Captive reinsurance undertaking: Absolute floor of EUR 1.3 million for a firmeneigenes Rückversicherungsunternehmen (section 1(2), item 5). BaFin's reinsurance notice of 1 March 2017 still states EUR 1.2 million for a captive reinsurer and EUR 3.6 million for other reinsurers. That notice says only the provisions in force at the time of the application are binding. The floor in force is section 1(2) of the Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung.
min_capital.How the minimum is set: Section 122 of the VAG defines the minimum capital requirement as the amount of eligible basic own funds below which policyholders and claimants would face an unacceptable level of risk if the undertaking continued. Section 1(1) of the Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung raises a calculated minimum capital requirement that is below 25 percent of the solvency capital requirement up to that 25 percent, and reduces one that is above 45 percent down to 45 percent. A capital add-on under section 301 is included in the solvency capital requirement for that test. Section 1(2) then sets absolute floors that the minimum capital requirement may not go below. Section 89 requires eligible own funds at least equal to the solvency capital requirement, and eligible basic own funds at least equal to the minimum capital requirement. At authorization, section 9 requires basic own funds covering the absolute floor and own funds covering the solvency capital requirement of the expected business.
min_capital.Health and property-casualty, including: Absolute floor of EUR 2.7 million where the undertaking does not cover risks in classes 10 to 15 of Annex 1 to the VAG (Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung, section 1(2), item 1).
min_capital.Property-casualty, including a captive i: Absolute floor of EUR 4 million where the undertaking covers a risk in at least one of classes 10 to 15 of Annex 1 (section 1(2), item 2).
min_capital.Life, including a captive insurer: Absolute floor of EUR 4 million (section 1(2), item 3).
min_capital.Reinsurance undertaking: Absolute floor of EUR 3.9 million (section 1(2), item 4).

tax_notes: The VAG and the Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung do not create a captive premium-tax exemption or a captive income-tax exemption. Section 23(1) of the Körperschaftsteuergesetz sets corporate income tax at 15 percent of taxable income for assessment years through 2027, then 14 percent in 2028, 13 percent in 2029, 12 percent in 2030, 11 percent in 2031, and 10 percent from 2032. The solidarity surcharge and municipal trade tax were not restated from a captive instrument in this review. Section 6(1) of the Versicherungsteuergesetz sets insurance premium tax at 19 percent of the premium excluding the tax, subject to the special rates in subsection (2), including 22 percent for fire and fire-business-interruption insurance. Section 4(1), item 1, exempts the payment of a reinsurance premium from that tax. A captive that writes direct insurance of risks situated in Germany is therefore in the premium-tax base unless another exemption in section 4 applies. A captive that writes only reinsurance is within the section 4(1) reinsurance exemption. No German equivalent of the French provision pour résilience was found in the statutes reviewed.
contact_name: Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht
types_allowed: Captive insurers (firmeneigene Versicherungsunternehmen), authorized as insurers under section 8 of the VAG and writing only the risks of the owner or of its group, as Directive 2009/138/EC, Article 13(2), defines them
Captive reinsurers (firmeneigene Rückversicherungsunternehmen), authorized only for reinsurance under section 8(4), as Article 13(5) of the Directive defines them
Stock corporations, including a European company (SE), mutual insurance associations, and public-law corporations and institutions
No protected-cell, incorporated-cell, or sponsored-captive regime is stated in the VAG or Kapitalausstattungs-Verordnung provisions reviewed
regulator_staff_count: BaFin reported 3,084 employees at 31 December 2025, of whom 2,067 worked in Bonn and 1,017 in Frankfurt. The organisation chart dated 1 October 2026 places captive supervision in Referat VA 46, within the insurance-supervision area. No headcount for that unit, or for insurance supervision alone, is published.

fees.licensing_incorporation: Item 19.2 of the Finanzdienstleistungsaufsichtsgebührenverordnung charges EUR 32,259 for granting the initial permission to carry on business under section 8(1) of the VAG. The regulation was made on 2 September 2021 and was last amended by Article 4 of the Act of 25 September 2026. The same item also covers certain other initial permissions, including a special purpose vehicle under section 168. BaFin's reinsurance notice of 1 March 2017 states a fee of EUR 10,000 under item 6.2 of the former FinDAGKostV. That notice tells the reader that only the law in force at the time of the application is binding. Commercial-register and notary formation costs are not set in item 19.2.
fees.annual_fees: No captive-specific annual euro amount is set in FinDAGebV item 19. BaFin recovers the cost of ongoing supervision by fees and by allocations charged to supervised undertakings. The allocation formula and the insurance-premium bands were not extracted from the cost-allocation regulation in this review.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No captive premium-tax rate is set in the VAG. Versicherungsteuergesetz section 6(1) sets the general rate at 19 percent of the premium excluding the tax. Section 4(1), item 1, exempts a reinsurance premium. Corporate income tax under Körperschaftsteuergesetz section 23(1) is 15 percent through the 2027 assessment year and then declines by one percentage point a year to 10 percent from 2032. No captive exemption from that tax was found.

annual_filing_requirements: Section 123 requires the minimum capital requirement to be calculated quarterly and the result reported to BaFin. A quarterly calculation of the solvency capital requirement is not required merely to set the minimum-capital boundaries. If an Article 129(3) boundary determines the minimum capital requirement, the undertaking explains why. Section 45 allows BaFin to exempt an undertaking from reports that delegated acts require more often than once a year, where the cost would be excessive relative to the risks and the information is still submitted at least annually. That exemption cannot remove the quarterly minimum-capital report. One factor in the proportionality test is whether the undertaking is a captive that covers only risks connected with the industrial or commercial group to which it belongs. Section 40 requires a solvency and financial condition report at least annually, no later than 14 weeks after the end of the financial year, approved by the management body before publication and sent to BaFin promptly after publication. The group report has six further weeks. Section 37 requires the annual accounts and the management report, both as drawn up and as adopted, and the audited solvency balance sheet and its audit report, to be submitted to BaFin without delay. Section 135 requires immediate notice if the minimum capital requirement is no longer covered or is expected to be uncovered within three months, and a realistic short-term financing plan within one month. BaFin's 2025 report said 469 insurers, Pensionskassen, and Pensionsfonds were under supervision. That total is not a captive count.

captive_administrator.name: Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht

licensing_speed: Sections 8 to 11 of the VAG do not state a number of days in which BaFin must grant or refuse an initial permission. Article 25 of Directive 2009/138/EC requires Member States to provide a judicial remedy where the supervisory authority has not decided the application within six months after receiving it. The article requires that remedy. It does not itself require the permission to be granted within six months. BaFin's insurance-authorization page asks applicants to arrange an early preliminary discussion through poststelle@bafin.de. The 2017 reinsurance notice does not state a processing time.

name: Gibraltar
summary: Gibraltar authorises captive insurers and captive reinsurers under the Financial Services (Insurance Companies) Regulations 2020, made under the Financial Services Act 2019. The consolidated regulations were last updated on 30 June 2026. A captive insurer is owned by a financial undertaking other than an insurer or reinsurer, or by a non-financial undertaking, and its purpose is to insure only the risks of the undertaking or undertakings to which it belongs, or of its group. A captive reinsurer is defined in the same way for reinsurance. Regulation 116 sets the absolute floor of the minimum capital requirement at £2,400,000 for non-life business, including a captive insurer, £3,500,000 where any of classes 10 to 15 is covered, £3,500,000 for life business, including a captive insurer, £3,500,000 for a reinsurer, and £1,200,000 for a captive reinsurer. The Gibraltar Financial Services Commission insurance-company page states the same floors. The minimum capital requirement must also lie between 25 and 45 percent of the solvency capital requirement, which regulation 91 calibrates at a 99.5 percent value-at-risk over one year. A company may be a protected cell company only with the Commission's written consent, and only if it is or will be a Gibraltar insurer or an authorised collective investment scheme, under the Protected Cell Companies Act 2001. Corporation tax on a company's taxable income is 15 percent for an accounting period. It was 10 percent through 31 July 2021 and 12.5 percent from 1 August 2021 until 30 June 2024. The pages reviewed do not publish a captive census, a staff count for insurance supervision, or a number of days in which an application must be decided.
legislation: Financial Services Act 2019, and the Financial Services (Insurance Companies) Regulations 2020
applicable_legislation: Financial Services Act 2019, dated 23 July 2019. Financial Services (Insurance Companies) Regulations 2020 (Legal Notice 2020/044), in operation from 15 January 2020, consolidated text last updated 30 June 2026. The captive insurer and captive reinsurer definitions are regulation 3(1). Permission and the scheme of operations are regulations 16 and 17. Own funds covering the solvency capital requirement are regulation 90. The 99.5 percent calibration is regulation 91(4). The minimum capital requirement and its absolute floors are regulations 115 and 116. Quarterly reporting of the minimum capital requirement is regulation 116(4). Protected Cell Companies Act 2001, including section 5 on cellular and non-cellular assets and section 11 on the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission's consent. Financial Services (Fees) Regulations 2020, consolidated through the amendments commencing on 1 April 2026 and 3 September 2026, Fee Block B1 and Schedules 1A and 1B. Financial Services (Insurance Supervisory Reporting) (Technical Standards) Regulations 2025, in operation from 31 January 2025, Article 2A, for the solvency and financial condition report deadline. Rates of Tax Rules 1989, made under the Income Tax Act 2010, rule 6, as updated to 1 July 2024, including the transitional rules 6C and 6D.

min_capital.Non-life, including a captive insurer: Absolute floor of £2,400,000, unless any of the risks in classes 10 to 15 is covered (regulation 116(1)(d)(i)).
min_capital.Life and non-life together: For an undertaking authorised for both life and non-life under regulation 63(2)(a) and (b), the absolute floor is the sum of the non-life and life floors. If the non-life business is limited to class 1 or 2, and gross written premiums for either life or non-life do not exceed 10 percent of total gross written premiums, the floor is the life amount in regulation 116(1)(d)(ii).
min_capital.Protected cell: Regulation 116 states the absolute floor for the insurance or reinsurance undertaking. It does not state a separate absolute floor for a protected cell. Section 5 of the Protected Cell Companies Act 2001 requires the directors to keep cellular assets separate from non-cellular assets and to keep each cell's cellular assets separate from the other cells.
min_capital.How the minimum is set: Regulation 115 requires eligible basic own funds covering the minimum capital requirement. Regulation 116(1) calibrates the linear calculation to an 85 percent value-at-risk of basic own funds over one year and then sets absolute floors. Without displacing those floors, regulation 116(3) requires the minimum capital requirement to be at least 25 percent and no more than 45 percent of the solvency capital requirement, including any capital add-on. Regulation 90 requires eligible own funds covering the solvency capital requirement. Regulation 91(4) sets that requirement at a 99.5 percent value-at-risk of basic own funds over one year. The Gibraltar Financial Services Commission insurance-company page states the same absolute floors and the same 99.5 percent solvency capital requirement.

tax_notes: Rule 6(1) of the Rates of Tax Rules 1989 charges corporation tax at 15 percent of a company's taxable income for an accounting period. A utility is charged 20 percent, and the Commissioner may charge 20 percent where a company has abused a dominant market position. Rule 6C keeps the rate at 10 percent through 31 July 2021 and at 12.5 percent from 1 August 2021 for an accounting period that straddled 1 August 2021. Rule 6D keeps the rate at 12.5 percent through 30 June 2024 and at 15 percent from 1 July 2024 for an accounting period that straddled 1 July 2024. The Rates of Tax Rules do not impose an insurance premium tax. No separate premium-tax instrument was retrieved.
contact_name: Gibraltar Financial Services Commission
types_allowed: Captive insurers, insuring only the risks of the owner or of the group, as regulation 3(1) defines them
Captive reinsurers, reinsuring only the risks of the owner or of the group

Captive insurers and captive reinsurers structured as protected cell companies, with the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission's written consent under section 11 of the Protected Cell Companies Act 2001
Life and non-life classes. Authorisation for a class, unless expressly restricted, also permits reinsurance in that class

fees.licensing_incorporation: Schedule 2, Fee Block B1, of the Financial Services (Fees) Regulations 2020 charges £10,500 for an application for Part 7 permission by a captive insurer, whether or not it is structured as a protected cell company. Approval of an additional protected cell is £3,500 if the Commission assesses it as non-complex, £11,000 if moderately complex, and £40,000 if complex. Unless the Commission agrees otherwise, the application is accompanied by the £3,500 and the balance of a higher fee is paid before the application is regarded as complete. The application fee is paid when the application is made. The fee regulation defines a captive insurer, for fee purposes, as an insurance or reinsurance company wholly owned by a parent which covers only risks of the group and no third-party risks. That fee definition is narrower than regulation 3(1) of the Insurance Companies Regulations. Incorporation fees of the company registry are not set in Schedule 2.
fees.annual_fees: Fee Block B1 charges a captive insurer, including one set up as a protected cell company, a base fee of £9,192 plus £2,625 for each cell, plus a gross-premium-income fee, a gross-technical-liabilities fee, a passporting fee, an internal-capital-model fee, and a matching-adjustment fee where those items apply. For a non-life captive the premium fee is £198 per £1,000,000 or part on the first £10,000,000 of gross premium income, then £164, £133, £100, and £65 per £1,000,000 or part on the higher bands. For a life captive the first band is £275 per £1,000,000 or part, then £253, £230, £206, and £185. The gross-technical-liabilities fee starts at £40 per £1,000,000 or part on the first £10,000,000 and then uses the lower rates in the schedule. Passporting is £1,030 on a services basis and £5,150 on an establishment basis. An approved internal capital model, and an approved matching adjustment, each add a monitoring fee of £51,500. A life captive insurer, including a protected cell company, also pays the Schedule 1B anti-money-laundering supervision fee of £4,017. Where the Commission undertakes group supervision, Schedule 1A adds £3,605, £11,330, or £41,200 according to the Commission's complexity assessment. The Schedule 1 fee is due within 28 days of the notice that permission has been granted and, after that, within 28 days from 1 April each year, unless the Commission agrees otherwise. A late fee draws an administrative fee of £250 and interest at 5 percent a year above base rate.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the Rates of Tax Rules 1989. Corporation tax is 15 percent of taxable income from 1 July 2024, after 10 percent through 31 July 2021 and 12.5 percent from 1 August 2021 to 30 June 2024.

annual_filing_requirements: Regulation 116(4) requires the minimum capital requirement to be calculated at least quarterly and the result reported to the Gibraltar Financial Services Commission. Article 2A of the Financial Services (Insurance Supervisory Reporting) (Technical Standards) Regulations 2025 requires the solvency and financial condition report to be disclosed no later than 70 business days after the financial year-end, and no later than 100 business days where the group report under regulation 233 applies. The same article requires submission of the own-risk-and-solvency-assessment report and the annual, half-yearly, and quarterly quantitative templates. Regulation 37 allows the Commission to limit reporting that would otherwise be more frequent than annual, where the burden is excessive for the risks and the information is still reported at least annually. That limit is not available merely because the undertaking is a captive, and regulation 116(4) is preserved. The regulations reviewed do not state that a board meeting must be held in Gibraltar.

captive_administrator.name: Licensed insurance managers. Fee Block B1 charges an insurance manager £524 a year for each captive insurer under management. The Gibraltar Financial Services Commission is the regulator, not the administrator of individual captives.

licensing_speed: The insurance-company page describes a three-stage application and says the Commission moves the file to the next stage when it is satisfied with the current stage. It does not state a number of days for a decision. Applicants request access to the submission system by email to authorisations@fsc.gi.

name: Guam
summary: Guam licenses captive insurance companies under Chapter 23 of Title 22 of the Guam Code Annotated. The Compiler of Laws source note says the chapter was added by Public Law 17-85 and later amended, including by Public Law 24-104 and by Public Law 27-54, which provided for protected cell companies. The Commissioner of Banking and Insurance, in the Department of Revenue and Taxation, is the licensing authority. A pure captive may insure only its parent and affiliated entities. A group captive may insure only its member organizations and their affiliates. An industrial insured captive may insure the industrial insureds in its group, their affiliates, and controlled unaffiliated businesses. An industrial insured uses an employee insurance manager or buyer, pays at least $15,000 of aggregate annual premium, and has at least 10 full-time employees. Minimum paid-in capital is $50,000 for a pure captive, $100,000 for a stock group captive, and $150,000 for a stock industrial insured captive. A rent-a-captive or protected cell captive starts at $150,000 for the first client or cell and rises by $150,000 for each additional client or cell, to a maximum of $750,000. Free surplus is $100,000 for a pure captive and $250,000 for a rent-a-captive or protected cell company. A captive that holds a Special Qualifying Certificate pays no Guam tax on premium or other insurance income except ad valorem tax on property used to produce income, and it pays its Guam income tax and then receives a full rebate under the certificate. Chapter 58 of Title 12 separately allows a 100 percent income-tax rebate on insurance underwriting income, and a business-privilege-tax abatement on insurance underwriting receipts, each for up to 20 years and renewable. Public Law 24-266, signed on 17 August 1998, amended that rebate section. It is not the captive licensing statute. The published captive regulation still states a $200 application fee and a $2,500 licence fee. The Compiler's chapter and the Department pages reviewed do not publish a captive census or a captive-unit headcount.
legislation: 22 GCA Chapter 23 (Captive Insurance Companies), added by Public Law 17-85
applicable_legislation: 22 GCA Chapter 23, sections 23101 to 23120, in the Compiler of Laws text. The source note says section 23101 was added by Public Law 17-85 and amended by Public Law 24-104, Public Law 27-54, and Public Law 27-88. Public Law 27-54 provided for protected cell companies. Capital and surplus are sections 23104 and 23105. Reports are section 23107. Examinations are section 23108. The premium and income-tax rule for a captive holding a Special Qualifying Certificate is section 23113, amended by Public Law 23-109 and Public Law 27-54. Chapter 16 of the captive insurance regulations published by the Compiler, citing rule-making authority in 22 GCA section 23101, sets the application, licence, and renewal fees. 12 GCA Chapter 58: section 58104(k) lists captive insurers among Qualifying Certificate applicants; section 58127.5 abates business privilege tax on insurance underwriting receipts; section 58128.4, added by Public Law 23-109 on 26 July 1996 and amended by Public Law 24-266 on 17 August 1998, provides the 100 percent income-tax rebate. The Compiler's source note for Chapter 23 does not print a calendar year for Public Law 17-85, and that public law was not separately retrieved.

min_capital.Pure captive: Unimpaired paid-in capital of not less than $50,000 (22 GCA section 23104(1)) and free surplus of not less than $100,000 (section 23105(1)).
min_capital.Group captive, stock: Unimpaired paid-in capital of not less than $100,000 (section 23104(2)). Section 23105 does not state a separate surplus figure for a group captive incorporated as a stock insurer.
min_capital.Group captive, mutual: Section 23105(2) requires free surplus of not less than $150,000 for a group captive incorporated as a mutual insurer. Section 23105(4) also requires free surplus of not less than $200,000 for a group captive incorporated as a mutual insurer. The statute states both amounts. Section 23104 does not set a paid-in-capital floor for a mutual.
min_capital.Industrial insured captive, stock: Unimpaired paid-in capital of not less than $150,000 (section 23104(3)) and free surplus of not less than $200,000 (section 23105(3)).
min_capital.Industrial insured captive, mutual: Free surplus of not less than $200,000 (section 23105(5)). Section 23104 does not set a paid-in-capital floor for a mutual.
min_capital.Rent-a-captive or protected cell: Unimpaired paid-in capital of not less than $150,000 for the first client or cell, increasing by $150,000 for each additional client or cell, to a maximum of $750,000 (section 23104(4)). Free surplus of not less than $250,000 (section 23105(6)). A protected cell is not a separate legal person (section 23106).
min_capital.Form of capital and surplus: Section 23104 requires the capital to be cash deposited in a Federal Reserve member bank licensed to do business in Guam and approved by the Commissioner. Section 23105 allows surplus to be cash, or an irrevocable letter of credit issued by a Federal Reserve member bank and approved by the Commissioner, or any other form acceptable to the Commissioner. The published captive regulation also accepts an irrevocable letter of credit, from a Guam-chartered bank or a Federal Reserve member bank approved by the Commissioner, as proof of compliance with both sections 23104 and 23105.

tax_notes: Section 23113 applies only to a captive that has been issued a Special Qualifying Certificate under 12 GCA Chapter 58. That captive pays no tax to the government of Guam on its premium or other insurance income, except ad valorem taxes on real and personal property used in the production of income. To the extent it must first pay its Guam income tax on that income, the tax is rebated in full under the certificate. Section 58128.4 allows a rebate of 100 percent of income tax paid on income from insurance underwriting inside or outside Guam, including income from investing funds derived from that underwriting, for up to 20 consecutive years, renewable for further periods of 20 years. For Guam risks and Guam policyholders, the beneficiary may not issue a policy directly to the policyholder and may issue it only through a licensed Guam insurance broker. Section 58127.5 abates business privilege tax, for up to 20 years and renewable for further periods of 20 years, on gross receipts from underwriting insurance risks in or out of Guam and on gross receipts from investing funds generated by that underwriting. The ordinary Qualifying Certificate income-tax rebate in section 58128.1 is up to 75 percent. The 100 percent insurance rebate is the specific rule. Section 58104(k) says a Qualifying Certificate may be issued for insurance issuance by a commercial insurer, reinsurer, or captive insurer that meets Title 22, Chapter 15, Article 3. Neither Chapter 23 nor Chapter 58 states that every captive receives the rebate without a certificate.
contact_name: Insurance, Securities, Banking and Real Estate Branch, Department of Revenue and Taxation
types_allowed: Pure captive insurance companies, limited to the parent and affiliated entities
Group captive insurance companies, stock or mutual, limited to member organizations and their affiliated entities
Industrial insured captive insurance companies, stock or mutual, covering the industrial insured group, their affiliates, and controlled unaffiliated businesses
Protected cell companies. A protected cell is an account of the company, not a separate legal person

Excess workers' compensation for the parent and affiliates, unless the law of the jurisdiction of the transaction prohibits it, and reinsurance of a qualified self-insured workers' compensation plan of the parent and affiliates

fees.licensing_incorporation: Section 23102(d) requires a non-refundable fee of $200 for examining, investigating, and processing the licence application. The captive regulation published by the Compiler repeats that $200 statutory application fee. Within 30 days after the Commissioner notifies an already incorporated applicant of approval, the regulation requires payment of a $2,500 licence fee. An applicant that is not yet incorporated pays the same $2,500 within 60 days after notice of approval, together with the incorporation filings. The statute does not state the $2,500 amount. Corporate filing fees of the Department are not set in Chapter 23.
fees.annual_fees: The published regulation says every licence expires on the 1 April following issuance. A captive that wants to renew applies on or before 1 March. The renewal is a letter identifying the company, evidence that it still meets sections 23104 and 23105, and a check for the $2,500 annual licence fee. The renewal is deemed granted unless the Commissioner rejects it in writing. Chapter 23 does not itself state an annual dollar fee. No later fee schedule changing the $200 or $2,500 amounts was retrieved.
fees.premium_tax_rate: A captive holding a Special Qualifying Certificate pays no Guam tax on premium or other insurance income except ad valorem property tax, and its Guam income tax on that income is paid and then rebated in full (22 GCA section 23113). Section 58128.4 allows a 100 percent income-tax rebate on insurance underwriting income for up to 20 years, renewable. Section 58127.5 abates business privilege tax on those underwriting receipts for up to 20 years, renewable. The rebate and abatement are certificate benefits. They are not stated as automatic for every captive.

annual_filing_requirements: Section 23107(a) requires a pure captive to submit a statement of financial condition, written on generally accepted accounting principles and audited by an independent certified public accountant, on or before the last day of the sixth month after the end of its fiscal year. A captive that is not a pure captive files, on or before 1 March, a National Association of Insurance Commissioners annual statement as of the preceding 31 December, verified by at least two principal officers, and a risk-based capital report. Its audit is due on or before 1 June. The statements include reserves for known claims and expenses, claims incurred but not reported and expenses, unearned premiums, and bad debts. An actuarial opinion on known-claim and incurred-but-not-reported reserves is included in the audited statements. For a captive other than a pure captive, that opinion is filed with the annual statement by 1 March. A late filing may be fined up to $500 a day and is a ground for suspension, revocation, or non-renewal. The Commissioner examines each captive at least once every three years, and may extend that period to five years if a comprehensive annual audit of satisfactory scope is performed by independent auditors the Commissioner approves. The captive pays the examination cost. At least one of not fewer than three incorporators must be a Guam resident. The captive maintains its principal place of business on Guam and appoints a resident registered agent. The published regulation still says every licensed captive files a National Association of Insurance Commissioners statement by 1 March and an audit by the end of the sixth month. Section 23107, as amended by Public Law 24-104 and Public Law 27-54, is the later filing rule for a pure captive. The Department's 4 February 2026 financial-statement letter is addressed to domestic and alien insurers under other sections of Title 22. Section 23115 says provisions of Title 22 outside Chapter 23 do not apply to captives except where Chapter 23 specifically refers to them.

captive_administrator.name: Insurance, Securities, Banking and Real Estate Branch, Regulatory Division, Department of Revenue and Taxation

licensing_speed: Chapter 23 does not set a number of days in which the Commissioner must grant or refuse a licence. Section 23102(f) says that if the Commissioner is satisfied the filings comply, the Commissioner may grant a licence. Section 23118 requires the Guam Captive Insurance Advisory Committee to recommend, within 30 days of receiving the information, whether the applicant should be licensed. The recommendation is advisory. The published regulation requires the $2,500 licence fee within 30 days after approval of an incorporated applicant, or within 60 days after approval of an applicant that still has to incorporate.

name: Guernsey
summary: Guernsey is a leading captive centre and the jurisdiction that pioneered the protected cell company. The Guernsey Financial Services Commission regulates insurers under the Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, using its own solvency rules rather than the EU Solvency II standard formula. At 31 December 2025 the Commission reported 196 non-cellular captives, after 8 additions and 9 surrenders in 2025. That 196 is not a total of all captives: of cells reported by type of insurer, 126 were classified as captives, after 13 additions and 9 surrenders. Pure/single-parent and group/association captive structures are permitted; the Commission does not publish a numerical breakdown of those types, a captive-only premium total, or a standard licensing time. At 31 December 2025 the international insurance sector comprised 44 PCCs, 222 PCC cells excluding insurance-linked securities, 14 ICCs and 46 ICC cells. Those PCC and ICC totals cover the wider international insurance sector and are not all captives. The same sector statistics also show 223 companies and 549 entities in total. The latest financial totals, for 2024, were £29.70 billion of gross assets, £12.62 billion of net worth and £5.19 billion of premiums written by international insurers as a whole, not by captives alone. Captive (re)insurers are Category 5 licensees. Category 6, including special purpose insurers and insurance-linked securities, is authorised separately and is not necessarily captive business. The capital floor is £100,000 for general business and £250,000 for long-term business, and the captive prescribed capital requirement is calibrated at a 90 percent confidence level over 12 months. Under the Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended, and States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance, company income tax is 0 percent on insurance income that is not domestic business and 10 percent on domestic insurance business. Reinsurance is outside the statutory definition of domestic business. Insurance supervision is carried out by the Banking and Insurance Division; the Commission does not publish a separate current headcount for insurance supervision alone. The Commission regulates insurers and does not administer individual captives. Most international insurers are administered by licensed insurance managers: 23 were authorised at 31 December 2025, and named managers are on the regulated-entities register. The Commission can pre-authorise later protected-cell-company cells on a product or class basis once the company and its first cell are approved, most often for fully collateralised special purpose insurer cells. It does not publish a 48-hour licensing standard. This profile was reviewed by the Commission (Shaun Green, 5 November 2026) against its published insurance statistics.
legislation: Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, and the Insurance Business (Solvency) Rules and Guidance, 2021
applicable_legislation: Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended; Insurance Managers and Insurance Intermediaries (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002; Insurance Business (Solvency) Rules and Guidance, 2021, including the 2024 amendment to the retail general-business capital floor; Insurance Business Rules and Guidance, 2021; Companies (Guernsey) Law, 2008 (Commission consent to incorporate a protected cell company or an incorporated cell company); Financial Services Commission (Fees and Administrative Penalties) Regulations, 2025; Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended (company standard rate 0 percent and intermediate rate 10 percent, per States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance).

min_capital.Category 5 captive, general business: £100,000 capital floor. Paid-up share capital must be at least the capital floor, and minimum shareholders' funds must be at least 75 percent of the capital floor. The minimum capital requirement cannot be below the capital floor. The prescribed capital requirement is set at a 90 percent confidence level over the next 12 months
min_capital.Category 5 captive, long-term business: £250,000 capital floor, with the same paid-up capital, shareholders' funds and 90 percent prescribed-capital tests
min_capital.Protected cell company that does not wri: The capital floor applies to the PCC as a whole. There is no separate capital floor for each cell or for the core. Each cell and the core has a notional minimum capital requirement calculated as if it were a stand-alone insurer, and the PCC minimum is the sum of those amounts, subject to the capital floor

tax_notes: Under the Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended, and States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance, the standard company rate of income tax is 0 percent. The 10 percent company intermediate rate applies to income from domestic insurance business, insurance intermediary business and insurance manager business. Insurance income that is not domestic business, including reinsurance (which the Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, excludes from domestic business), is taxed at 0 percent. Income from Guernsey land and buildings is taxed at 20 percent. Insurance is an economic-substance category for accounting periods after 1 January 2019. Revenue Service company-tax guidance does not state a separate premium-tax rate.
contact_name: Guernsey Financial Services Commission
types_allowed: Category 5 captive insurers and reinsurers. Pure/single-parent and group/association structures are permitted; a separate count is not published
Protected cell companies and cells used for captive business
Incorporated cell companies and cells used for captive business
regulator_staff_count: Banking and Insurance Division. No separate current headcount for insurance supervision is published.

fees.licensing_incorporation: Under the Financial Services Commission (Fees and Administrative Penalties) Regulations, 2025, as summarised by the GFSC: Category 5 captive insurer or reinsurer application fee £7,850 for a company, PCC core or ICC core. A Category 5 cell of a PCC or ICC is £2,520. A Category 6 special purpose insurer cell is £110. A pro-rata annual fee is invoiced when the licence is issued.
fees.annual_fees: Due 31 January for licences in effect on 1 January. Category 5 captive insurer or reinsurer, including a PCC core or ICC: £7,850. Category 5 cell: £2,520. Category 6 company: £7,725. Category 6 cell that is not a special purpose insurer: £2,520. Special purpose insurer cell: £110. Dormant cell: £205. Change of general representative: £600. Change of controller: £2,760. Category 6, including special purpose insurers and insurance-linked securities, is a separate licence category and is not necessarily captive business.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Under the Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended, and States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance, company income tax is 0 percent on insurance income that is not domestic business and 10 percent on domestic insurance business. That guidance does not state a separate premium-tax rate.

annual_filing_requirements: Licensed insurers must deposit an annual return with the Commission within four months beginning on the close of the financial year (Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, section 37). The return includes the regulatory solvency assessment. Each insurer must also complete an Own Risk and Solvency Assessment at least annually and submit the resulting Own Solvency Capital Assessment with the annual return. The general representative is responsible for filing. A late return attracts an administrative financial penalty. Licensed insurance managers and insurance intermediaries deposit their annual return within six months of the financial year-end. Guernsey company income tax returns are filed separately with the Revenue Service; the 2025 corporate return is due 30 November 2026.

captive_administrator.name: Licensed insurance managers (23 authorised at 31 December 2025). Named managers are listed on the GFSC regulated-entities register. The Commission is the regulator, not the administrator of individual captives.

licensing_speed: No published standard timeline. PCC cells may be pre-authorised on a product or class basis after the PCC and its first cell are approved; this route is most commonly used for fully collateralised special purpose insurer cells.
